teaching.rule: French has three words for 'the': le before a masculine singular noun, la before a feminine singular noun, and les before any plural. In front of a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u or a silent h), both le and la shrink to l' with an apostrophe. When the little words à (to / at) or de (of / from) land next to le or les, they fuse into one word: au, aux, du, des. French also keeps 'the' where English drops it: for languages (J'apprends le français, though right after parler it is usually dropped: je parle anglais), for things in general (J'aime le chocolat) and for habits like 'on Mondays' (le lundi).

examples.note: train is masculine and singular, so it takes le.
gare is feminine and singular, so it takes la.
Plural nouns take les whatever their gender; the final s of les is silent.
avion starts with a vowel, so le shrinks to l' to stop two vowel sounds bumping together.
à + le is never said as two words; it must fuse into au.

contrast.note: NOT 'J'aime chocolat': English drops 'the' for things in general, French must keep it.
NOT 'Je vais à le parc': à and le never sit side by side; they fuse into au.
NOT 'l'amis': only le and la shrink before a vowel; les stays les, and its s sounds like z before a vowel (lé-za-mi).

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers drop the article for general statements ('J'aime musique') or leave à and le apart ('à le parc'); keep the article (J'aime la musique) and fuse à + le into au.

probes.exEn: The station is far from here.

items.note: Use le before a masculine singular noun starting with a consonant; the noun's gender, not its meaning, decides.
Use la before a feminine singular noun starting with a consonant; maison is feminine, so la.
Use les before any plural noun, masculine or feminine; the s is silent unless a vowel follows.
le shrinks to l' before a vowel or silent h so two vowel sounds don't clash; the h of hôtel is silent.
la also shrinks to l' before a vowel; université is still feminine even though you can't see la.
à + le must fuse into au; you can never say 'à le'.
à + les fuses into aux; the x sounds like z before a vowel (au-zé-lèves).
de + le fuses into du; here it shows who something belongs to, like the English 's.
de + les fuses into des; it looks like the 'some' des but here it means 'of the'.
items.exEn: Here are the names of the streets.

items.note: Languages take le in French where English uses no article at all.
le + a day name means every such day, a habit; French uses the article instead of 'on'.
To talk about cats in general, French says les chats; English drops the article but French keeps it.

teaching.rule: To say 'a' or 'an', use un before a masculine noun and une before a feminine noun; un and une also mean the number one. For more than one thing, French needs des ('some'), even when English says nothing: 'I have friends' is J'ai des amis. After a negative like ne... pas, un, une and des all shrink to de: Je n'ai pas de voiture (the one exception is after être: ce n'est pas une voiture). Unlike English a / an, French never changes un or une because of a following vowel; you just say the n: une idée.

examples.note: vélo is masculine, so un.
clé is feminine, so une.
More than one, so des; English can drop 'some' but French cannot drop des.
After ne... pas, un turns into de.
un doubles as the number one; French does not have a separate word.

contrast.note: NOT 'J'ai amis': French needs des in front of plural things even when English says nothing.
NOT 'pas un chien': after a negative the article becomes de.
NOT 'un amie': French does not switch une to un before a vowel the way English switches a to an; say u-na-mie.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'J'ai amis' or 'Je n'ai pas un chien'; use des for plural things (J'ai des amis) and de after a negative (pas de chien).

items.note: Use un before a masculine noun; it also means the number one.
Use une before a feminine noun; the final e makes the n sound, unlike un.
Plural 'a' is des; English drops 'some' but French must keep des.
chien is masculine, so un; the final n of un is nasal, not fully pronounced.
voiture is feminine, so une; most nouns ending in -ure are feminine.
homme starts with a silent h, so the n of un links to it: u-nomme.
des is required before plural things even where English says just 'flowers'.
idée is feminine; French keeps une before a vowel and links the n: u-ni-dée.
un is the number one as well as 'a'; before the vowel of an the n links: un-nan.
items.exEn: I've lived here for one year.

items.note: After ne... pas with avoir and most verbs, un / une / des all shrink to de; 'je n'ai pas un vélo' is wrong.
The negative de shrinks to d' before a vowel or silent h, just like le and la: pas d'amis, pas d'idée.
items.exEn: I don't have any friends here.

items.note: un turns a general thing into one countable item: un café is one cup.
items.ex: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.

teaching.rule: Every French noun is either masculine or feminine, even objects and ideas, and this decides the little word in front: le / un for masculine, la / une for feminine. Gender has nothing to do with meaning, so always learn a noun together with its article, like la lune or le livre. The ending gives strong clues: -tion, -té, -ette and -ure are almost always feminine; -age, -ment, -eau and -isme are almost always masculine. A final -e is NOT a safe feminine clue (le problème, le musée).

examples.note: Ends in -tion, so feminine; almost every -tion word is.
Ends in -age, so masculine.
Ends in -té, so feminine.
Ends in -ment, so masculine.
Gender is not logical: the sun is masculine and the moon feminine; learn the article with the word.

contrast.note: NOT 'la problème': it ends in -e but is masculine, like le système and le thème.
NOT 'le plage': -age is usually masculine, but plage, page and image are feminine.
NOT 'la musée': the -ée ending looks feminine, but musée and lycée are masculine.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers assume any word ending in -e is feminine ('la problème'); learn each noun with its article and trust ending patterns like -tion (feminine) and -ment (masculine) rather than the last letter alone.

items.note: livre is masculine, so le; there is no clue in the ending, so learn the article with the word.
Nouns ending in -tion are almost always feminine, so la question.
Nouns ending in -age are nearly always masculine (le fromage, le garage), so le voyage.
Nouns ending in -ment are masculine, so le moment.
Ends in -e but is masculine: words of Greek origin in -ème (le système, le thème) are masculine.
Many abstract nouns in -eur are feminine (la couleur, la peur, la chaleur), while -eur words for people like le vendeur are masculine.
People nouns change form with the person: le chanteur becomes la chanteuse, and the article changes too.
People nouns follow natural gender: une femme is feminine, un homme masculine.
Nouns ending in -té are feminine (la santé, la liberté, la beauté).
items.ex: Le sport est bon pour la santé.
items.exEn: Sport is good for your health.

items.note: An exception: -age is usually masculine, but plage, page and image are feminine; learn these with their article.
items.exEn: Shall we go to the beach?

items.note: Ends in -ée like many feminine words, but musée and lycée are masculine.
Gender is not logical: the sun is le soleil (m) and the moon is la lune (f); always learn the article with the noun.

teaching.rule: A subject pronoun is the little word that says who does the action: je (I), tu (you, one person you know well), il (he / it), elle (she / it), on (we, casual), nous (we), vous (you: polite, or more than one person), ils (they), elles (they, all female). A French verb almost always needs one; you cannot say just 'parle'. Before a vowel or silent h, je becomes j' (j'aime). For 'they', use ils unless every person in the group is female, then elles. Things get il or elle depending on the noun's gender: la voiture is elle.

examples.note: je is the doer; it is lowercase unless it starts the sentence.
tu for one friend, family member or child.
The same question to a stranger, or to several people, uses vous.
on is the casual spoken 'we'; the verb takes the same form as with il.
A mixed group takes ils, even with only one man in it.

contrast.note: NOT 'Je aime': je loses its e before a vowel and glues on with an apostrophe.
NOT for a mixed group: elles only when every person is female; otherwise ils.
NOT 'he is raining': il also means 'it' for weather and for masculine things.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers use il for every 'it' and ils for every 'they'; il / elle follow the noun's gender (la voiture → elle) and elles is only for an all-female group.

items.note: je is only ever the subject (the doer) and stays lowercase unless it starts the sentence.

items.en: I love (je shortened before a vowel)
items.note: je drops its e before a vowel or silent h and glues on with an apostrophe: j'adore, never 'je adore'.
tu is for one person you know well: a friend, family member or child.
items.exEn: And you, where do you live?

items.note: il is 'he' for a person and 'it' for any masculine noun, like le livre; spoken French often names the person first, then repeats it with il.
items.ex: Mon frère, il travaille à Paris.

items.note: elle is 'she' for a person and 'it' for any feminine noun, like la voiture; as with il, speech often names the person, then adds elle.
on is the everyday spoken 'we' and also 'people / one'; it takes the same verb form as il.
items.ex: Ce soir, on mange au restaurant.
items.exEn: Tonight we're eating at the restaurant.

items.note: nous is the standard 'we', used in writing and careful speech; its verb ends in -ons.
items.ex: Le week-end, nous restons à la maison.
items.exEn: At the weekend we stay at home.

items.en: you (formal, or more than one person)
items.note: vous is for someone you address politely and for any group of people; its verb ends in -ez.
ils covers any group that has at least one male in it, and any masculine things.
items.ex: Mes parents, ils habitent à Marseille.

items.note: elles is only for a group made entirely of women or feminine things; the s is silent.
ce is the subject of c'est and means 'it' or 'that', not 'he'; it shrinks to c' only when est follows directly, and stays ce when ne comes between (ce n'est pas).
items.exEn: So, it's not a big deal.

items.note: moi is the stressed form used for emphasis or after 'et'; the verb still needs je: Moi, je...

teaching.rule: Most French verbs end in -er, like parler (to speak), and they all follow one pattern. Take off -er to get the stem (parl-), then add the ending that matches the subject: je parle, tu parles, il / elle / on parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils / elles parlent. Four of these (parle, parles, parle, parlent) sound exactly the same, so listen for the pronoun to know who is doing it. The French present covers both English 'I speak' and 'I am speaking'; there is no separate -ing form.

examples.note: One French form covers both English forms.
The -es ending is silent; it sounds just like habite.
-ons is said like the nasal 'on'.
-ez is said like é.
-ent is completely silent; ils écoutent sounds like il écoute.

contrast.note: NOT 'Je suis parle' or 'Je suis parlant': do not build am + -ing; the simple present already means it.
NOT 'nous mangons': manger keeps an e after the g so the g stays soft before -ons.
NOT 'vous parles': vous always takes -ez, even when talking to just one person politely.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers try to build 'I am speaking' with être ('Je suis parle'); just use the simple present, je parle, which means both 'I speak' and 'I am speaking'.

items.note: Stem parl- plus -e for je; the final e is silent, so it sounds like 'parl'.
Stem plus -es for tu; the -es is silent, so it sounds exactly like je parle.
Stem plus -e for il, elle and on; it sounds the same as je parle and tu parles.
items.ex: Mon voisin, il parle très vite.

items.note: Stem plus -ons for nous; -ons is pronounced like the nasal 'on'.
items.ex: À la maison, nous parlons anglais.

items.note: Stem plus -ez for vous; -ez sounds like é and is used even for one person addressed politely.
items.exEn: Excuse me, do you speak English?

items.note: Stem plus -ent for ils and elles; the -ent is completely silent, so it sounds like il parle.
aimer starts with a vowel, so je shrinks to j'; the -e ending is silent.
habiter starts with a silent h, so je still shrinks to j' as before a vowel.
items.ex: En ce moment, j'habite à Lyon.
items.exEn: At the moment, I live in Lyon.

items.note: travailler drops -er and adds -e; the -ill- is said like a y sound: tra-va-ye.
items.ex: Le samedi, je travaille à la maison.
items.exEn: On Saturdays I work at home.

items.note: manger keeps an extra e before -ons so the g stays soft (like j), unlike 'mangons'.
Stem aim- plus -es for tu; the s is silent, so it sounds like j'aime.
items.exEn: Tell me, do you like chocolate?

items.note: One French form covers both 'she watches' and 'she is watching'; no -ing form exists.
items.ex: Le soir, elle regarde la télé.
items.exEn: In the evening, she watches TV.

teaching.rule: Four verbs turn up in almost every French sentence: être (to be), avoir (to have), aller (to go) and faire (to do / make). They do not follow the regular -er pattern, so learn each form as its own word. Look at the subject first (je, tu, il/elle/on, nous, vous, ils/elles) and pick the form that goes with it. être: je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont. avoir: j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont. aller: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont. faire: je fais, tu fais, il fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils font. Listen for the endings: ils sont (they are) starts with a clear s, while ils ont (they have) links as 'il-ZON'.

examples.note: être + adjective for a state; suis looks nothing like the infinitive être, so memorize it as a word.
The nous form of avoir keeps the av- of the infinitive; the s of nous links into avons ('nou-za-von').
aller changes completely in the ils form: vont, not 'allent'.
faites is one of only three vous forms in French that do not end in -ez (with êtes and dites).

contrast.note: Age uses avoir (have), not être: never 'je suis vingt ans'.
ont (avoir) is not sont (être): ont has no s sound at the start and links to ils as 'il-zon'.
Hot, cold, hungry, thirsty and afraid all use avoir, not être + adjective.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'je suis faim' or 'je suis vingt ans' because English uses 'to be'; hunger, thirst, age, heat and cold all take avoir: j'ai faim, j'ai vingt ans.

probes.ex: Ils font la cuisine ce soir.
probes.exEn: They are doing the cooking tonight.

items.note: être (to be) is the most used verb in French; its je form suis looks nothing like the infinitive, so learn it as a word.
The s of es is silent, so tu es sounds like 'tu è'; use it only with someone you call tu.
The nous form of être; the final -es is silent, so it sounds like 'som'.
The s of vous links into êtes ('vou-ZÈT'); this is one of only three vous forms that do not end in -ez.
sont starts with a clear s sound, which is how you tell it apart from ils ont (they have).
je shrinks to j' before the vowel of ai; French also uses j'ai for age and hunger (j'ai faim), where English uses 'I am'.
The il/elle/on form of avoir is just a, said 'ah'; do not confuse it with à (to, at), which carries an accent.
The s of ils links into ont, so it sounds like 'il-zon'; that z sound is your clue that this is avoir, not être.
aller (to go) is irregular from the very first form: vais, said 'vè'; French uses it both for 'I go' and 'I am going'.
items.exEn: I am going to the market.

items.note: The nous and vous forms of aller (allons, allez) are the only ones that still look like the infinitive.
items.exEn: We are going to the cinema.

items.note: faire covers both 'do' and 'make'; je fais, tu fais and il fait all sound the same ('fè').

items.en: you do / you make (formal or several people)
items.note: Not 'vous faisez': faites is irregular, one of only three vous forms not ending in -ez.

teaching.rule: Prepositions are the little words that link a verb or noun to a place, a person or a purpose: à (to / at), de (of / from), dans (in), sur (on), sous (under), avec (with), pour (for), chez (at someone's place). Put them right before the noun or pronoun, as in English, and never leave one hanging at the end of a sentence. Watch the fusions: à + le becomes au, de + le becomes du, and à + les / de + les become aux / des.

examples.en: I am going to the station.
examples.note: à marks the destination; with la it stays as two words (à la).
chez + a person or profession means 'at their place / office'; English needs the possessive 's.

examples.fr: Le chat est sous la chaise.
examples.en: The cat is under the chair.
examples.note: sous (under) is the opposite of sur (on); they differ by one vowel, so listen carefully.

contrast.en: I am going to the cinema.
contrast.note: Not 'à le cinéma': à + le always fuses into au.
Do not translate word for word as 'à la maison de Marie'; chez does the whole job.
The preposition stays in front of the question word; French never strands it at the end.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers write 'à le' or 'de le' as two words; French always fuses them into au and du (je vais au marché, je viens du bureau).

probes.ex: Le chien est sous la table.
probes.exEn: The dog is under the table.
We are having dinner at my parents' place.
She is going to the market.

items.note: à points to a destination or location; the accent tells it apart from a (has).
de shows origin or possession (le livre de Paul); it shrinks to d' before a vowel.
dans means physically inside something; the final s is silent and the vowel is nasal ('dan').
items.ex: Les clés sont dans la boîte.
items.exEn: The keys are in the box.

items.note: sur means on top of a surface; say the u with rounded lips so it does not turn into sous (under).
items.ex: Le livre est sur la table.
items.exEn: The book is on the table.

items.note: sous (said 'soo') means below something; only the vowel separates it from sur (on).
items.ex: Le chat dort sous le lit.
items.exEn: The cat is sleeping under the bed.

items.note: avec ends in a consonant you actually pronounce ('a-vèk'), unlike the silent finals of dans and sous.
items.exEn: I am having dinner with my friends.

items.note: sans is the opposite of avec; after sans you usually drop the article: sans sucre, not 'sans du sucre'.
items.ex: Un café sans sucre, s'il vous plaît.

items.note: pour introduces a purpose or the person something is meant for; after pour, use the stressed pronoun (toi, moi).
items.exEn: It is a present for you.

items.note: chez + person means at that person's home, shop or office; there is no one-word English equivalent.
items.ex: Ce soir, je reste chez moi.
items.exEn: Tonight I am staying at home.

items.note: entre places something between two others; the final e is silent ('antr').
items.ex: La pharmacie est entre la banque et la poste.
items.exEn: The pharmacy is between the bank and the post office.

items.en: at the park / to the park (à + le)
items.note: à and le can never sit side by side: they fuse into au before a masculine noun starting with a consonant (au parc, au bureau); before a vowel it stays à l' (à l'hôtel).
items.exEn: The children are at the park.

items.note: devant is a preposition on its own, no de after it: devant la gare, not 'devant de la gare'.
items.exEn: I am waiting in front of the station.

teaching.rule: To make a noun plural, add -s to the written word, but that -s is silent: in speech you hear the plural in the article, le / la becoming les (sounds 'lay') and un / une becoming des ('day'). Nouns ending in -eau or -eu add -x instead (gâteaux, jeux), most nouns in -al switch to -aux (animaux), and nouns already ending in -s, -x or -z do not change at all (un bus, des bus). A few are simply irregular and must be memorized: un œil becomes des yeux.

examples.note: You hear the plural in les, not in the silent -s of chats.
-eau takes -x, not -s; gâteaux sounds exactly like gâteau.
-al becomes -aux, and here the sound changes too: ani-MO.

contrast.note: bus already ends in -s, so nothing is added; only the article changes.
cheveu (-eu) takes -x; cheval (-al) becomes chevaux: two different rules, easy to mix up.
Not 'des œils': the plural of œil is completely irregular.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers pronounce the final -s of plurals ('chatss'); in French it is silent, and only les / des (or a number) tells the listener the noun is plural.

items.note: Add -s to chat, but say it exactly like the singular; only deux and the written -s show it is plural.
la becomes les in the plural, and les (said 'lay') is the part you actually hear; the -s of maisons is silent.
Nouns in -eau add -x, never -s; the x is silent, so gâteaux sounds like gâteau.
items.ex: Elle fait des gâteaux pour la fête.
items.exEn: She is making cakes for the party.

items.note: Nouns in -eu also add -x: un jeu, des jeux (both said 'jeu').
items.ex: Les enfants adorent les jeux vidéo.

items.note: Most nouns in -al drop the -al and take -aux; this is one of the few plurals that changes the sound ('o').
items.ex: Il y a des animaux dans le jardin.
items.exEn: There are animals in the garden.

items.note: cheval follows the -al to -aux rule: cheval, chevaux; do not add -s.
journal (newspaper) is another -al noun: un journal, des journaux.
items.ex: Il lit deux journaux par jour.
items.exEn: He reads two newspapers a day.

items.note: bus already ends in -s, so singular and plural are spelled and said the same; only les / des tells you which.
items.ex: Les bus passent toutes les dix minutes.
items.exEn: The buses come every ten minutes.

items.note: prix ends in -x, so it never changes: un prix, des prix.
The irregular plural of un œil; the pair œil / yeux has to be memorized because no rule produces it.
monsieur is really mon + sieur, so both halves go plural: messieurs (and madame becomes mesdames).
Most -ou nouns just add -s (des trous), but seven take -x: bijoux, cailloux, choux, genoux, hiboux, joujoux, poux.
items.ex: Elle porte des bijoux en or.

teaching.rule: To say 'not', wrap the verb in two words: ne before it and pas after it: Je ne parle pas (I do not speak). Before a vowel or silent h, ne shrinks to n' (Je n'aime pas). Swap pas for jamais (never), plus (no longer), rien (nothing) or personne (nobody) to change the meaning. After a negative the articles un / une / du / des all become de: je n'ai pas de voiture; the one exception is être, where the article stays (ce n'est pas un problème). In casual speech the ne often disappears, but always write it.

examples.note: ne + verb + pas; French needs no 'do' to make a negative.

examples.en: She does not live here anymore.
examples.note: plus takes the place of pas, and ne becomes n' before the silent h of habite.
des becomes de (here d' before a vowel) after the negative.

contrast.note: Spoken shortcut that drops ne; fine with friends, wrong in anything written.

contrast.en: I do not have a dog.
contrast.note: Not 'pas un chien': after pas the article un becomes de.
After être the article stays (un, not de); the de rule applies to other verbs.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers use only one half of the negative and keep the article ('je pas ai un chien'); say Je n'ai pas de chien, with both ne and pas and de instead of un.

probes.ex: Je ne bois jamais de café.

probes.exEn: I do not know anyone here.

items.note: The two halves wrap around the verb, ne in front and pas behind; English 'do not' is just ne... pas.
ne loses its e and becomes n' when the verb starts with a vowel or silent h: n'aime, n'habite.
items.exEn: I do not like the cold.

items.note: jamais replaces pas; do not use both (never 'ne... pas jamais').
items.ex: Il ne mange jamais de viande.

items.note: plus replaces pas to say something has stopped; in this negative use the final s of plus is silent ('plu').
items.exEn: She no longer lives in Paris.

items.note: rien replaces pas; English says 'I do not see anything' but French says 'I do not see nothing'.
personne replaces pas to mean nobody (the same word with une means 'a person', so the ne is what makes it negative).
items.ex: Il n'y a personne dans la rue.
items.exEn: There is nobody in the street.

items.note: After a negative, un / une / du / des all shrink to de: pas de voiture, pas de pain, pas d'amis.
items.exEn: I do not have a car.

items.note: Add encore right after pas; note that encore alone means 'still' or 'again', so it needs the negative to mean 'yet'.
items.ex: Le dîner n'est pas encore prêt.

items.note: Before an infinitive the two halves stay together in front of the verb: ne pas + verb, as on signs and after merci de.
items.ex: Merci de ne pas fumer ici.

items.note: To agree with a negative, French says 'me not either'; moi aussi (me too) is for agreeing with a positive.
items.ex: Elle n'aime pas le sport, et moi non plus.
items.exEn: She does not like sport, and neither do I.

items.note: When a question is negative, French answers 'yes' with si, not oui; oui would sound like you agree with the negative.
items.ex: Tu ne viens pas ? — Si, je viens !
items.exEn: Aren't you coming? — Yes, I am!

items.note: du tout strengthens pas; on its own, Pas du tout ! is a common short answer meaning 'Not at all!'.
items.ex: Je n'aime pas du tout le poisson.
items.exEn: I do not like fish at all.

teaching.rule: There are three ways to ask a yes / no question. Easiest: say the statement with a rising voice, Tu viens ? Neutral: put est-ce que in front, Est-ce que tu viens ? Formal: flip the verb and subject with a hyphen, Viens-tu ? For information, start with the question word (qui who, où where, quand when, comment how, pourquoi why, combien how much / how many, quel which) and then use one of those three patterns; in casual speech the question word can also go at the end: Tu habites où ? French has no 'do / does', and there is a space before the question mark.

examples.note: est-ce que does the job of English 'do'; the words after it keep normal statement order.
Question word first, then the verb, then the subject; with a short verb like est, this flip is normal even in casual speech.
Casual spoken style: statement order with the question word (quoi) at the end.

contrast.note: 'What' at the start of a question is qu'est-ce que, not quoi; quoi only goes after the verb or a preposition (Tu fais quoi ? Avec quoi ?).
A bare Quoi ? sounds rude; use Pardon ? or Comment ? to ask someone to repeat.
English 'what' before a noun is quel / quelle, not que or quoi.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers add 'do / does' ('do tu viens ?') or translate 'What?' as a blunt Quoi ?; French just uses a rising voice or est-ce que, and Pardon ? is the polite 'What?'.

probes.exEn: How many sugars do you want?

probes.ex: Est-ce que tu aimes le fromage ?

items.note: Put est-ce que (literally 'is it that') in front of any statement to make it a question; nothing else moves.
items.ex: Dis-moi, est-ce que tu viens ce soir ?
items.exEn: Tell me, are you coming tonight?

items.note: The most casual question is the plain statement said with a rising voice; in writing, only the question mark shows it.
items.ex: Tu viens ? On part dans cinq minutes.
items.exEn: Are you coming? We leave in five minutes.

items.en: Do you speak English? (formal, verb first)
items.note: Formal questions flip the verb and the subject pronoun and join them with a hyphen; keep this for vous and for writing.
items.exEn: Excuse me, do you speak English?

items.note: qui asks about a person and never changes form; the final i is said 'ee' (kee).
'What' at the start of a question is this three-word block, said 'kès-ke'; que on its own is rare in speech.
quoi is 'what' when it comes after the verb or a preposition (Tu fais quoi ? Avec quoi ?), never at the start of a sentence.
items.exEn: What are you doing this weekend?

items.note: où (with the accent) asks about a place; without the accent, ou means 'or', and both are said 'oo'.
quand asks about time; the final d is silent, so it sounds like 'kan', and the d links as a t sound before a vowel (quand est-ce que: 'kan-tès-ke').
comment asks about manner; French asks your name with it, literally 'how do you call yourself'.
pourquoi is pour + quoi, literally 'for what'; answer it with parce que (because).
combien covers both 'how much' and 'how many'; before a noun add de: combien de personnes.
'What' or 'which' directly before a noun is quel; it agrees with the noun (quelle heure, quels jours), and age is asked with it plus avoir.

teaching.rule: Words like my, your and his go in front of the noun and change to match THAT noun, not the owner: mon / ton / son before a masculine singular noun (mon frère), ma / ta / sa before a feminine singular noun (ma sœur), mes / tes / ses before any plural (mes amis). For our, your (formal or plural) and their, use notre, votre, leur, and simply add -s before a plural noun: nos, vos, leurs. Before a vowel sound, use mon / ton / son even with a feminine noun so the words flow: mon amie, not ma amie.

examples.note: son because chien is masculine; the owner being a woman changes nothing.

examples.en: Paul is looking for his sister.
examples.note: sa because sœur is feminine, even though the owner is a man.
notre becomes nos before a plural noun; there is no gender change for our / your / their.
amie is feminine but starts with a vowel, so ma switches to mon to avoid two vowels bumping together.

contrast.note: 'mine' on its own is à moi, not mon: mon / ma / mes must always sit in front of a noun.
Not 'sa frère': frère is masculine, so it takes son even though the owner is female.
leur never becomes 'leure' for a feminine noun; it only adds -s when the noun is plural.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers choose son or sa by the owner's sex ('sa' for her), but French chooses by the noun's gender, so 'her brother' is son frère and 'his sister' is sa sœur.

items.note: Use mon when the noun is masculine singular; the owner's gender plays no part.
Use ma when the noun is feminine singular (clé is feminine: une clé) and starts with a consonant.
mes covers every plural noun, masculine or feminine; the final s links to a following vowel (mes amis).
items.exEn: I'm going to my parents' place.

items.note: ton is the informal 'your' (when you say tu) before a masculine singular noun, or any noun starting with a vowel sound: ton amie.
ta is the informal 'your' for one feminine singular noun (une voiture); use ton before a masculine one.
tes is the informal 'your' before any plural noun, whatever its gender.
son goes with a masculine singular noun and means his OR her: the owner's gender is not shown.
sa goes with a feminine singular noun; 'his sister' is sa sœur because sœur is feminine.
items.exEn: Paul is looking for his sister.

items.note: ses is his / her before a plural noun; it is not 'their', which is leurs.
notre is 'our' before one noun of either gender (notre maison, notre fils); before a plural noun it becomes nos.
notre becomes nos before a plural noun; there is no separate feminine form.
votre is 'your' when you say vous, for one noun of either gender; before a plural noun it becomes vos.
leur adds -s before a plural noun; it never changes for gender.
amie is feminine, but before a vowel sound ma switches to mon so the two vowels don't clash.

teaching.rule: Use c'est (that is / it is) to point at or identify something: c'est + a name, c'est + un / une / mon + noun, or c'est + an adjective for a general comment (c'est bon). Before a plural noun it becomes ce sont: ce sont mes amis. Use il y a (there is / there are) to say that something exists or is somewhere; it never changes for plural. When you describe a person with a job, nationality or adjective and no un / une in front, use il est / elle est instead: il est médecin, elle est française. The negative of il y a is il n'y a pas de.

examples.note: c'est identifies who or what something is; it is followed by a name or an article + noun.

examples.fr: Il y a un chat sur la table.
examples.en: There's a cat on the table.
examples.note: il y a states that something exists; it stays exactly the same with a plural: il y a des chats.

examples.fr: Il est professeur. / C'est un professeur.
examples.note: no article after il est; as soon as you add un / une, you must switch to c'est.
for a general comment, c'est + adjective in the masculine form, whatever you are talking about.

contrast.note: là says where someone is; il y a says something exists. Don't use il y a to mean 'he is there'.

contrast.fr: Elle est avocate. / C'est une bonne avocate.
contrast.en: She's a lawyer. / She's a good lawyer.
contrast.note: No article after elle est; adding une (and an adjective) forces c'est.
With an adjective and no article, use ils sont, not ce sont; ce sont needs a noun: ce sont des Français.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers translate 'there is' word for word ('là est') or say 'il est un ami' when identifying; use il y a for existence and c'est un ami whenever un / une follows.

probes.ex: Dans le frigo, il y a du lait.
Ce sont mes amis Paul et Léa.
probes.exEn: They're my friends Paul and Léa.

items.note: ce + est becomes c'est; it points at or identifies something and is followed by a name, an article + noun, or an adjective.
The plural of c'est, used before a plural noun (ce sont mes amis), never before an adjective. In casual speech you will hear c'est mes amis, but ce sont is the correct form.
ce only shortens to c' before est; in the negative, ne slips in between, so the full ce comes back: ce n'est pas.
A fixed expression meaning something exists; il here does not mean 'he', and the form is the same for one thing or many.
items.ex: Dans ma rue, il y a une boulangerie.
items.exEn: In my street there's a bakery.

items.en: there is no / there aren't any
items.note: The negative of il y a; after pas, un / une / des all become de.
items.ex: Désolé, il n'y a pas de wifi ici.

items.note: Put est-ce que in front to turn il y a into a question; que shortens to qu' before il.
items.ex: Pardon, est-ce qu'il y a une pharmacie près d'ici ?
items.exEn: Excuse me, is there a pharmacy near here?

items.note: The everyday way to ask what something is; literally 'what is it that it is', said as one block.
c'est + adjective makes a general comment; the adjective stays masculine singular even if you're talking about a feminine thing.
For a job with no article, French uses il est / elle est, and drops the 'a': il est médecin.
As soon as un / une (and an adjective) come before the job, you must use c'est, not il est.
items.ex: Je te le recommande, c'est un bon médecin.
items.exEn: I recommend him, he's a good doctor.

items.en: there you go / there it is
items.note: Points something out or hands it over; also used to finish a story ('and that's that').
Presents something close to you or introduces a person; voilà works too, but voici is the classic word for introductions.
items.exEn: Hello, this is my sister Léa.

teaching.rule: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, so always learn the word together with its little word: le pain, la maison. Before a vowel sound both le and la shrink to l' (l'eau, l'argent), so for those words memorise the gender separately. These nouns come up dozens of times a day, and many appear inside fixed phrases (à la maison, au travail, c'est la vie), so learn the phrase as one block.

examples.note: French says 'to the house' where English says 'home': à la maison is the block to remember.
eau is feminine but takes l' before a vowel; de l' means 'some' here.
English drops 'the', French keeps it: le temps.

examples.fr: Il y a beaucoup de gens.
examples.note: gens is always plural, like 'people', and never takes a number in front.

contrast.en: the day (a date) / the day (its length)
contrast.note: jour counts days (trois jours); journée is the whole day as you live it (bonne journée !).

contrast.en: time (in general) / the time (on the clock)
contrast.note: Ask for the clock time with heure (Quelle heure est-il ?), not temps.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'je vais à maison' or 'j'ai pas temps' without the article; French keeps le / la in these set phrases: à la maison, le temps.

probes.ex: Il y a beaucoup de gens ici.
probes.exEn: There are lots of people here.

items.note: Feminine; fois counts occasions (une fois, deux fois), unlike temps, which is time in general.
Feminine (une eau), but la shrinks to l' before the vowel; the plural is les eaux.
Feminine; en ville means 'in town' with no article, unlike à la maison, which keeps it.
Masculine; à + le contracts to au, so 'to work' is au travail.
Masculine; one word for both time and weather, and the final -ps is silent.
Masculine despite the l' (mon argent); it also means silver. Note the nasal -en- sound.
Masculine; use jour for counting days and dates, and journée for how the day goes (bonne journée).
Feminine; handy when you don't know a word, and the base of quelque chose (something).
Masculine; the female friend is l'amie, spelled with an extra e but pronounced the same.
Feminine; French keeps the article where English drops it: c'est la vie.
Always plural and masculine in everyday use; the final s is silent.
items.ex: Il y a beaucoup de gens ici.
items.exEn: There are lots of people here.

items.note: Masculine even though it ends in -e; keep both accents, and un coup de téléphone is 'a phone call'.

teaching.rule: Count with un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix, and build bigger numbers with vingt, cent and mille. Numbers never change form, with one small exception: vingt and cent take an -s when multiplied and nothing follows (quatre-vingts, deux cents) but drop it if another number follows (deux cent dix); mille never changes. To give the clock time say Il est + number + heure(s), then add the minutes: Il est huit heures dix; 'half past' is et demie, 'noon' is midi. For dates use le + number + month (le trois mai); only the first of the month uses premier. Final consonants of numbers are usually silent, but they come back before a vowel: trois heures sounds like 'trwa-zeur'.

examples.note: Always il est for the time, and heures takes an -s from two o'clock on; the s of trois links to heures.

examples.fr: Il est huit heures et demie.
examples.note: demie ends in -e because heure is feminine; after midi it would be et demi.
The t of vingt is silent here but sounds before a vowel: vingt ans.
Dates take le + number + month with no 'of'; premier is only for the 1st, then le deux, le trois...

contrast.fr: Quelle heure est-il ? / Quel temps fait-il ?
contrast.en: What time is it? / What's the weather like?
contrast.note: heure is clock time; temps is time in general or the weather, never used to ask the hour.

contrast.en: a hundred euros / two hundred euros
contrast.note: cent alone means 'a hundred' with no 'un' in front; it takes an -s when multiplied and nothing follows (deux cents), but not in deux cent dix.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'un cent' or 'un mille' for a hundred / a thousand; French drops the 'un': cent euros, mille euros.

probes.ex: Il est huit heures et demie.

items.note: The final s is silent, but it links as a z sound before a vowel: trois heures.
The x is silent (say 'deuh'), but it links as a z sound before a vowel: deux heures, deux ans.
Said 'deess' on its own, 'dee' before a consonant (dix personnes) and 'deez' before a vowel (dix euros).
The q is pronounced ('sank'); it is one of the few numbers whose final consonant is usually heard.
Nasal 'kanz'; useful for times too, since a quarter past is et quart but a quarter of an hour is quinze minutes.
items.ex: Le train part dans quinze minutes.
items.exEn: The train leaves in fifteen minutes.

items.note: Silent -gt at the end; the t sounds before a vowel, so vingt ans is 'van-tan'.
No 'un' in front: cent on its own already means one hundred.
Never takes an -s and never takes 'un' in front: deux mille, mille euros.
items.exEn: This bike costs a thousand euros.

items.en: the hour / the time (on the clock)
items.note: Feminine (une heure); the h is silent, so la shrinks to l'. Use it to ask the time, not temps.
Add et demie after heure(s) for half past; demie has an -e because heure is feminine.
items.ex: Il est huit heures et demie.

items.note: No heures after midi: Il est midi. Midnight is minuit.
Dates use plain numbers (le deux mai), except the 1st, which is le premier.
items.ex: Mon anniversaire est le premier mai.
items.exEn: My birthday is the first of May.

items.note: One word with an apostrophe inside; the final syllable sounds like 'dwee'.
Ends in a nasal -ant sound with a silent t; it can go at the start or the end of the sentence.

teaching.rule: Family words come in male / female pairs, and the article tells you which is which: le père / la mère, le frère / la sœur, le fils / la fille. You will almost always say them after mon, ma, mes (my), so learn each word with its possessive: ma mère, mon père, mes parents. Two words do double duty: fille means both daughter and girl, and femme means both wife and woman; the context makes it clear.

examples.note: mère is feminine, so ma; the accent grave on è gives the open 'eh' sound.
fils ends in an s that IS pronounced ('feess'), and the word is the same in the plural.
A hyphenated pair where both halves take an -s in the plural.
femme after a possessive means wife; on its own une femme is a woman.

contrast.note: The same word: after ma / sa it means daughter, elsewhere it means girl.
parents in everyday French means mother and father only; wider family are les proches or la famille.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'mon mère' or 'ma père' by matching the possessive to themselves; match it to the noun instead: ma mère (feminine), mon père (masculine).

items.note: Feminine, so it takes ma; the è gives an open 'eh' sound.
Masculine, so it takes mon; rhymes with mère and frère.
Masculine; the plural is mes frères, and the -ère ending rhymes with père and mère.
Feminine; the joined œ is pronounced like the 'eu' in fleur, and can be typed as oe.
Plural; in everyday French it means mother and father, not relatives in general.
The same word for a boy or a girl; only the article shows the gender (un enfant / une enfant).
Masculine; unusually, the final s is pronounced, and the plural (les fils) looks and sounds the same.
Feminine; also means girl, and the -ille ends in a 'y' sound ('fee-y').
Hyphenated; both parts take an -s in the plural. Grandfather is le grand-père, grandmother la grand-mère.
Feminine; the -ille ends in a 'y' sound like fille, and en famille means 'with the family'.
Masculine; the i at the end is a clean 'ee' with no y sound.
The same word as woman; after sa / ma it means wife. Pronounced 'fam', not 'fem'.

teaching.rule: Learn every food word with its little word for 'the' (le for masculine, la for feminine, les for plural), because that word tells you its gender. The two verbs you will hear with food are manger (to eat: je mange, elle mange) and boire (to drink: je bois, elle boit). When you eat or drink SOME of something, put du (masculine), de la (feminine) or des (plural) before the food: du fromage, de la viande, des légumes; when you like or hate a food in general, use le / la / les: J'adore le fromage. Listen for du / de la before a food word: it means 'some', and French says it even where English says nothing.

examples.fr: Je bois du café le matin.
examples.en: I drink coffee in the morning.
examples.note: bois = drink; café is masculine, so 'some coffee' is du café, and French says the 'some' even though English leaves it out.
mange = eats; viande is feminine, so 'some' is de la, not du.
Liking a food in general uses le / la / les, never du / de la.

examples.fr: Je voudrais un thé, s'il vous plaît.
examples.en: I would like a tea, please.
examples.note: Ordering one cup uses un / une, just like 'a' in English.

contrast.note: French never drops the little word before a food noun: say Je mange du fromage.

contrast.fr: Je ne mange pas de la viande.
contrast.note: After a negative (ne ... pas), du / de la / des all shrink to plain de: Je ne mange pas de viande.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'Je mange pommes' with no article; French always needs one, so say Je mange des pommes (some apples) or J'aime les pommes (apples in general).

probes.ex: Le fromage est sur la table.
probes.exEn: The cheese is on the table.

probes.ex: Elle boit du lait au petit-déjeuner.
Le repas est prêt à midi.
probes.exEn: The meal is ready at noon.

items.note: Masculine; the same word also means the café where you drink it, so un café is 'a coffee' at the counter.
items.ex: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: I would like a coffee, please.

items.note: Masculine; the accent on é makes the vowel sound like the 'ay' in 'say'.
items.ex: Elle boit du thé le soir.
items.exEn: She drinks tea in the evening.

items.note: Masculine; the final t is silent, so it sounds like 'lay'.
Masculine; words ending in -age are almost always masculine, so learn it as le fromage.
Feminine, so 'an apple' is une pomme; la pomme de terre (earth apple) is a potato.
Masculine; the -ain ending is a nasal vowel, so the n is not fully sounded, and 'some bread' is du pain.
items.ex: Je mange du pain avec du fromage.
items.exEn: I am eating bread with cheese.

items.note: Masculine; the -in ending is a nasal vowel, so the n is not fully pronounced, and vin rouge / vin blanc put the colour after the noun.
items.ex: Un verre de vin rouge, s'il vous plaît.
items.exEn: A glass of red wine, please.

items.note: Masculine; it is both the animal and the food, and the double s keeps it distinct from le poison (poison).
items.ex: On mange du poisson ce soir.

items.note: Feminine, so 'some meat' is de la viande.
items.ex: Je ne mange pas de viande.

items.note: Masculine (un légume); usually met in the plural because you eat several, and les / des / tes before it tells you it is plural.
Masculine; the final s is silent and the word does not change in the plural (les repas).
Literally 'the little lunch', with a hyphen; le déjeuner alone is lunch, so do not drop petit.
items.ex: Je prends mon petit-déjeuner à sept heures.
items.exEn: I have my breakfast at seven o'clock.

teaching.rule: Rooms and furniture are ordinary nouns, so learn each one with le or la to fix its gender. To say where something IS, use dans (in) or sur (on) plus the room or object: dans la cuisine, sur la table. To say you are GOING TO a room, use à + the article, and remember that à + le squashes into au: Je vais au salon, but Je vais à la cuisine. Words starting with a vowel take l' instead of le or la: l'appartement.

examples.fr: Le chat dort dans la chambre.
examples.en: The cat is sleeping in the bedroom.
examples.note: dans + la chambre: being 'in' a room is dans, and chambre keeps its feminine la.

examples.en: We're going to the living room.
examples.note: Going TO a room is à + the article, and à + le salon becomes au salon; French never says à le.
appartement starts with a vowel, so 'the apartment' is l'appartement, but 'an apartment' is un appartement.

examples.fr: Ferme la porte, s'il te plaît.
examples.note: Ferme is the order you give a friend or family member: just the verb, with no word for 'you' in front (Ferme = close, Ouvre = open, Regarde = look).

contrast.note: à and le always merge into au: au salon.
chambre is feminine, so it is la chambre; the le or la you learn with each room decides every la / une / ma that goes in front of it.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'la salle de bains' to mean the toilet, but in France the toilet is usually a separate room called les toilettes, so ask for les toilettes when you need one.

probes.ex: Ma chambre est au premier étage.
probes.exEn: My bedroom is on the first floor.

probes.ex: Il fait chaud, ouvre la fenêtre.
Le lit est dans la chambre.
probes.exEn: The bed is in the bedroom.

items.note: Feminine; the same word also means cooking, so faire la cuisine is 'to do the cooking'.
Feminine; it means the room you sleep in (also a hotel room), not any room.
Feminine because salle (room) is feminine; bains is plural and often written without the s (salle de bain).
items.ex: La salle de bains est à gauche.
items.exEn: The bathroom is on the left.

items.note: Masculine; 'in the living room' is dans le salon, and 'to the living room' is au salon because à + le becomes au.
items.ex: La télé est dans le salon.
items.exEn: The TV is in the living room.

items.note: Feminine; do not confuse it with the verb form je porte (I wear / I carry).
Feminine; the hat accent (ê) marks an old s, so it is the cousin of English 'fenestration'.
Feminine; spelled like English but pronounced 'tabl' with no 'ay' sound.
items.ex: Le repas est sur la table.
items.exEn: The meal is on the table.

items.note: Feminine; the ch is a soft 'sh' sound, as in almost every French word starting with ch.
Masculine with a silent t; 'to bed' is au lit because à + le becomes au.
Masculine (un appartement), but the vowel start forces l' instead of le; note the double p and single r.
Feminine; the -on ending is a nasal vowel, and à la maison means 'at home'.
Always plural in French (so the verb is sont, not est); in France the toilet is usually its own small room, separate from the bathroom.

teaching.rule: Colours are describing words, and in French they come AFTER the thing they describe: une robe rouge, not une rouge robe. They also change shape to match the noun: add -e for a feminine noun (vert / verte, noir / noire) and -s for a plural (des chats noirs). A few colours never change: orange, marron, and any colour with clair or foncé after it (bleu clair). Listen for the -e: verte has a hard 't' sound at the end that vert does not.

examples.note: Colour after the noun; chat is masculine, so noir stays in its plain form.
voiture is feminine, so noir gains an -e (the pronunciation barely changes).
orange comes from the fruit, so it never takes -e or -s.
Adding clair (light) or foncé (dark) freezes the colour: no -e even for a feminine noun.

contrast.note: English puts the colour first; French puts it after: une robe rouge.
chemise is feminine, and blanc has the irregular feminine blanche: une chemise blanche.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers put the colour before the noun and forget to match it; say un pantalon noir but une robe noire, with the colour after and the -e added for feminine words.

probes.exEn: She is wearing a red dress.

probes.ex: Mon voisin a une voiture blanche.
probes.exEn: My neighbour has a white car.

probes.ex: Le parc est très vert au printemps.
probes.exEn: The park is very green in spring.

items.note: Ends in -e already, so it has the same form for masculine and feminine; only add -s for plurals.
items.exEn: I am eating a red apple.

items.note: Adds -e for feminine (une robe bleue) and -s for plural (bleus); the eu sound is like 'uh' with rounded lips.
Feminine is verte, and adding the -e makes the silent t suddenly heard; la pomme is feminine, so the blank needs verte.
Already ends in -e, so the masculine and feminine forms are identical.
Feminine is noire (une voiture noire); the oi spelling is pronounced 'wa', so noir sounds like 'nwar'.
Irregular feminine blanche: the silent c becomes a 'sh' sound when the -e is added; la neige is feminine, so the blank needs blanche.
Feminine is grise (the s becomes a 'z' sound); the masculine plural stays gris because it already ends in s.
items.ex: Le ciel est gris ce matin.
items.exEn: The sky is grey this morning.

items.note: Named after the fruit, so it never changes: des chaussures orange with no -s.
Same form for both genders since it ends in -e; as a noun, une rose is the flower.
Named after the chestnut, so it never changes; use it for eyes and objects (for brown hair French uses a different word, châtain).
Feminine is violette with a double t, which makes the final t audible; un pull is masculine, so here it stays violet.
items.exEn: She is wearing a purple sweater.

items.note: clair means light and foncé means dark; a colour followed by either word is frozen and never takes -e or -s, even after a feminine word like chemise.

teaching.rule: To say something hurts, use J'ai mal à + the body part: J'ai mal à la tête. Remember that à + le squashes into au (au bras) and à + les into aux (aux pieds). For everyday actions French says 'the' instead of 'my' or 'your' and adds a small word that shows whose body it is, me (myself) or toi (yourself): Je me lave les mains (I wash my hands), Lave-toi les mains (wash your hands). Learn the odd plural: un œil (one eye) but les yeux (eyes).

examples.note: Literally 'I have pain at the head'; tête is feminine, so à la stays as it is.
bras is masculine, so à + le becomes au; French says 'the arm', not 'his arm', after avoir mal.
Describing someone uses avoir + les + body part + colour, with the colour matching the plural (bleus).
à + les pieds becomes aux pieds; 'I have cold at the feet' is how French says it.

contrast.note: à le is never allowed; it must contract to au bras.
French says Je me lave les mains: the small word me already shows the hands are mine, so the body part takes les, not mes.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers translate 'my head hurts' word for word as 'Ma tête fait mal'; the natural French is J'ai mal à la tête, with avoir mal à + the article.

probes.ex: Il tient le stylo dans la main.
probes.exEn: He is holding the pen in his hand.

probes.ex: J'ai mal au dos depuis hier.
probes.exEn: My back has been hurting since yesterday.

items.note: Feminine; the hat accent (ê) gives an open 'eh' sound and the final e is silent, so it sounds like 'tet'.
Feminine even though it ends in a consonant; the -ain ending is a nasal vowel, so the n is not fully sounded, and les tells you the blank is plural (mains).
Masculine; the final s is silent and stays in the plural (les bras), so the word never changes shape.
Feminine; the j is soft like the s in 'measure', and the -amb- is a nasal vowel; for a state like 'broken' (not an action) ma jambe is normal.
Masculine with a silent d; à + les pieds becomes aux pieds (so the blank is plural), and à pied means 'on foot'.

Masculine; the joined œ is pronounced like the 'eu' in peur, and par cœur means 'by heart'.

teaching.rule: The verb for wearing clothes is porter (which also means 'to carry'): Je porte une robe. To put something on, say mettre (Mets ton manteau); the opposite, taking it off, is enlever. Each item of clothing has a gender, so learn it with le or la, and note that some words are singular in French but plural in English: un pantalon is one pair of trousers. Colours go AFTER the clothing word and match it: une chemise blanche, des chaussettes rouges.

examples.note: porter for 'wear'; pantalon is singular, so the colour noir is singular too.

examples.en: She is wearing a red dress.
examples.note: robe is feminine, so 'a' is une, and rouge sits after the noun.

examples.fr: Mets ton manteau, il fait froid.
examples.en: Put on your coat, it's cold.
examples.note: mettre = put on; Mets is the friendly command form, and ton matches the masculine manteau.
chaussures is plural and feminine, so 'some shoes' is des chaussures.

contrast.note: One pair is un pantalon, singular; the plural means several pairs.
avoir = own, porter = wear; Elle porte une robe tells you what she has on right now.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'mes pantalons' for one pair because 'trousers' is plural in English; say Je porte un pantalon, singular, and for 'she has a red dress on' use porter (Elle porte une robe rouge), not avoir.

probes.exEn: He is wearing a white shirt.
It's raining, put on your coat.

items.note: Singular in French for one pair, so 'my trousers' is mon pantalon; the plural means several pairs.
Feminine; a false friend, since it is an ordinary shirt, not a nightdress, and un chemisier is the women's blouse.

Masculine; words ending in -eau add -x in the plural (les manteaux), not -s.
Masculine; like manteau it ends in -eau, so the plural is les chapeaux with an x.
items.exEn: He is wearing a grey hat.

items.note: Feminine; the u is the tight French 'u' (say 'ee' with rounded lips).
items.exEn: She is wearing a long skirt.

items.note: Masculine; borrowed from English 'pullover' and cut short, so the u sounds like the French u, not like 'pull'.
Feminine plural, built on chausser (to put on footwear); the colour after it takes -s to match: des chaussettes rouges.
items.exEn: I am putting on red socks.

items.note: Feminine; a false friend, since it is a jacket, not a vest (an undershirt is un maillot de corps).
Masculine; borrowed from English and often written t-shirt, so both spellings are accepted.
items.exEn: He is wearing a blue T-shirt.

items.note: A regular -er verb that means both 'to wear' and 'to carry', so je porte covers both; with clothes it always means wear.
items.exEn: I am wearing a black jacket.

teaching.rule: French never says 'it IS hot' for weather. For a general condition use 'il fait' + a describing word: il fait beau, il fait chaud, il fait froid. For things you can see in the sky use 'il y a du / de la / des' + a noun: il y a du soleil, il y a du vent, il y a des nuages. Rain and snow are one-word verbs: il pleut, il neige. The 'il' is the impersonal 'it', not 'he'. To ask, say 'Quel temps fait-il ?'

examples.note: General condition: il fait + describing word.

examples.fr: Il y a du vent ce matin.
examples.note: A noun (vent) needs 'il y a du', not 'il fait'.

examples.en: It's been raining since this morning.
examples.note: Rain is a verb on its own: pleuvoir -> il pleut.

contrast.note: Sounds like 'I'm turned on / fired up'. For feeling hot say 'J'ai chaud' (I have heat).

contrast.en: It / he is cold (an object or a person)
contrast.note: 'Il est froid' describes a thing, e.g. cold coffee. Weather is 'il fait froid'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'c'est chaud' or 'il est chaud' for the weather and 'je suis froid' for feeling cold; the fixes are 'il fait chaud' and 'j'ai froid'.

probes.ex: Mets un manteau, il fait froid.
probes.exEn: Put on a coat, it's cold.

probes.ex: Il y a du vent, ferme la fenêtre.
Quel temps fait-il à Lyon aujourd'hui ?
probes.exEn: What's the weather like in Lyon today?

items.note: General weather uses 'il fait' + describing word; 'beau' here means fine, not handsome.
items.ex: Il fait beau, on mange dehors.
items.exEn: The weather is nice, we're eating outside.

items.note: Weather with 'il fait'; feeling cold yourself is 'j'ai froid'.
items.ex: En hiver, il fait froid à Paris.
items.exEn: In winter it's cold in Paris.

items.note: Weather with 'il fait'; never 'il est chaud' for the weather.
items.ex: En été, il fait très chaud ici.
items.exEn: In summer it's very hot here.

items.note: The opposite of 'il fait beau'; 'mauvais' means bad.
items.ex: Il fait mauvais, on reste à la maison.
items.exEn: The weather is bad, we're staying home.

items.note: From the verb pleuvoir; it only exists with impersonal 'il' and the -eu- sounds like the vowel in 'peu'.
From the verb neiger, again with impersonal 'il'.
Masculine, so 'it's sunny' is 'il y a du soleil' (du = de + le).
items.ex: Il y a du soleil ce matin.

items.note: Masculine; because it is a noun you say 'il y a du vent', not 'il fait vent'.
items.ex: Il y a beaucoup de vent aujourd'hui.
items.exEn: There's a lot of wind today.

items.note: Feminine noun; 'il pleut' is the verb, 'la pluie' is the thing falling.
Masculine; plural 'des nuages' gives 'il y a des nuages' for 'it's cloudy'.
items.ex: Il y a un gros nuage gris.

items.note: Feminine, short for 'météorologie'; French people say 'la météo' for the forecast on TV or an app.
items.ex: Je regarde la météo avant de sortir.
items.exEn: I check the forecast before going out.

items.note: Literally 'what weather does it make?'; 'temps' means weather here, not time.
items.exEn: What's the weather like in Nice?

teaching.rule: Learn every place with its little word (le, la or l') because you need it to say 'to / at'. 'À' (to, at) merges with 'le' to give 'au': au marché, au parc. With feminine words it stays 'à la': à la gare, à la banque. Before a vowel it is 'à l'': à l'école, à l'hôpital. So when you hear 'au', the place is masculine; 'à la', it is feminine.

examples.note: 'gare' is feminine, so 'à la' stays as it is.
'à + le' must become 'au'.
Vowel start: 'à l''. Note French keeps the article where English drops it ('at school').

contrast.note: 'à' + 'le' always contracts to 'au': Je vais au marché.
False friend: a library is 'la bibliothèque'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'à le' instead of 'au' and drop the article ('à école'); always keep le/la/l' and contract 'à le' to 'au'.

probes.ex: J'achète du pain à la boulangerie.
probes.exEn: I buy bread at the bakery.

probes.ex: Il y a de bons fruits au marché.
probes.exEn: There's good fruit at the market.

probes.ex: Le train part de la gare à huit heures.
probes.exEn: The train leaves the station at eight.

items.note: Feminine, so 'to the station' is 'à la gare'; a bus station is 'la gare routière'.
items.ex: On se retrouve devant la gare à huit heures.
items.exEn: We're meeting in front of the station at eight o'clock.

items.note: Masculine; a false friend, it is not a magazine (that is 'le magazine').
items.ex: Le magasin ferme à dix-neuf heures.

items.note: Masculine, so 'at the restaurant' is 'au restaurant'; the final -t is silent.
items.ex: On dîne au restaurant ce soir.
items.exEn: We're having dinner at the restaurant tonight.

items.note: Feminine (une école); French keeps the article: 'à l'école' where English says 'at school'.
items.ex: Les enfants vont à l'école à pied.

items.note: Masculine (un hôpital); the h is silent so 'le' becomes 'l''; plural is 'les hôpitaux'.
items.exEn: My sister works at the hospital.

items.note: Feminine; 'à la banque' for 'at the bank' (money only, a river bank is different).
items.ex: Je retire de l'argent à la banque.
items.exEn: I withdraw money at the bank.

items.note: Masculine, so 'in the park' is 'au parc'; the final -c is pronounced.
items.exEn: The children are playing in the park.

items.note: Feminine; French says 'dans la rue' (in the street), not 'sur'.
items.ex: J'habite dans une petite rue calme.
items.exEn: I live on a quiet little street.

items.note: Masculine (un aéroport); vowel start means 'à l'aéroport'.
items.exEn: The taxi is going to the airport.

items.note: Masculine; 'au marché' for 'at the market'; most towns have an open-air one on set days.
items.ex: J'achète des légumes au marché le samedi.
items.exEn: I buy vegetables at the market on Saturdays.

items.note: Feminine; shops ending in -erie are feminine (la boucherie, l'épicerie), and so is 'la pharmacie'.
items.ex: J'achète une baguette à la boulangerie.
items.exEn: I buy a baguette at the bakery.

items.note: Feminine; 'la poste' is the post office, while 'le poste' (masculine) means a job or position.
items.ex: Je vais à la poste pour envoyer un colis.
items.exEn: I'm going to the post office to send a parcel.

teaching.rule: To ask the way, start with 'Excusez-moi' or 'Pardon', then 'Où est la gare ?' (Where is the station?) or 'Pour aller à la gare, s'il vous plaît ?' (How do I get to the station?). Answers use two verbs: tournez (turn) and continuez (keep going): 'Tournez à gauche', 'Continuez tout droit'. Position words are followed by 'de': 'à côté de la gare', 'en face de l'école'; 'de + le' becomes 'du' (en face du parc).

examples.en: Excuse me, where is the station?
examples.note: Polite opener + 'où est' + the place.

examples.fr: Tournez à droite, puis continuez tout droit.
examples.en: Turn right, then keep going straight.
examples.note: The -ez ending is the polite 'you' form used with strangers.

examples.fr: C'est en face de la banque.
examples.note: 'en face de' needs 'de' before the place.

contrast.note: 'droite' (with -e, sounds 'drwat') is right; 'droit' (no -e, sounds 'drwa') is straight.
'près', 'à côté', 'en face', 'loin' all need 'de' before the place: près de la gare.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers mix up 'à droite' (right) with 'tout droit' (straight) and drop the 'de' after près / à côté / en face / loin.

probes.exEn: Keep going straight to the bridge.

probes.ex: L'hôtel est à côté de la gare.
probes.exEn: The hotel is next to the station.

probes.ex: Tournez à gauche après la pharmacie.

items.note: 'la gauche' is the left-hand side; you always keep the 'à' when giving a direction.
items.ex: Tournez à gauche au feu rouge.
items.exEn: Turn left at the traffic light.

items.note: 'droite' ends in -e and the -t is heard ('drwat'); do not confuse with 'tout droit'.
items.ex: La banque est à droite, après le pont.
items.exEn: The bank is on the right, after the bridge.

items.note: No -e on 'droit' and the final -t is silent ('too drwa'); it means keep going in a straight line.
items.ex: Continuez tout droit jusqu'à la place.
items.exEn: Keep going straight ahead to the square.

items.note: Always followed by 'de' + the place; 'de + le' becomes 'du' (près du parc).
items.ex: L'hôtel est près de la gare.
items.exEn: The hotel is near the station.

items.note: The opposite of 'près de'; also needs 'de' before the place.
items.ex: Le parc n'est pas loin de l'école.
items.exEn: The park isn't far from the school.

items.note: Sounds like 'ee-see'; use it for the spot where you are standing.
Points to a place away from you; the hyphen joins 'là' (there) and 'bas' (down/along).
items.ex: Le cinéma est là-bas, au bout de la rue.
items.exEn: The cinema is over there, at the end of the street.

items.note: Literally 'at the side of'; the 'de' is part of the phrase.
items.ex: La poste est à côté de la banque.
items.exEn: The post office is next to the bank.

items.note: 'face' is the front, so 'en face de' means facing / across from; keep the 'de'.
items.ex: Le café est en face de l'église.
items.exEn: The café is opposite the church.

items.note: 'le coin' is the corner; 'au' = à + le, and 'de' links it to the street.
items.ex: La boulangerie est au coin de la rue.
items.exEn: The bakery is at the corner of the street.

items.note: The vous form of 'tourner' used as an instruction to a stranger; with a friend say 'tourne'.

items.en: how do I get to (asking the way)
items.note: Literally 'to go to'; French asks the way with this unfinished sentence plus 's'il vous plaît'.
items.ex: Pardon, pour aller à la gare, s'il vous plaît ?
items.exEn: Excuse me, how do I get to the station, please?

teaching.rule: To say what someone does, use 'être' + the job with NO 'a / an': Je suis médecin, Il est boulanger (never 'je suis un médecin'). Many job words change for a woman: -eur becomes -euse (serveur / serveuse), -er becomes -ère (boulanger / boulangère), -ien becomes -ienne (pharmacien / pharmacienne); some like 'médecin' and 'professeur' stay the same. When you add a comment, switch to 'c'est un / une': C'est un bon médecin.

examples.note: No 'une' after 'je suis'; the -e ending shows the speaker is female.
Plain job statement: 'il est' + job, no article.
Feminine form of 'infirmier': -er becomes -ère.

contrast.note: With je suis / il est / elle est a job takes no article: Je suis professeur.
After 'c'est' you say 'C'est un médecin' or 'C'est un bon médecin'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers add 'un / une' after 'je suis' when naming their job ('je suis un avocat'); say 'je suis avocat', and keep 'un / une' only after 'c'est'.

probes.ex: Je suis infirmière à l'hôpital de Lille.
probes.exEn: I'm a nurse at the Lille hospital.

probes.ex: Le boulanger ouvre à six heures.
Mon cousin est avocat à Lyon.
probes.exEn: My cousin is a lawyer in Lyon.

items.note: Often shortened to 'le prof / la prof'; the feminine 'la professeure' exists but many women still say 'je suis professeur'.
items.ex: Mon professeur de français est sympa.

items.note: One form for both men and women ('elle est médecin'); 'le docteur' is the title you use to address them.
items.ex: Elle est médecin dans un hôpital.
items.exEn: She's a doctor in a hospital.

items.note: Masculine form; a female student is 'l'étudiante', and the final -t is only heard in the feminine.
items.exEn: I'm a student at the university.

items.note: Masculine -eur ending; call him 'Monsieur', never 'garçon', in a modern café.
The -eur ending becomes -euse for a woman, a pattern shared by vendeuse and coiffeuse.
Masculine (un ingénieur); the feminine 'ingénieure' is spelled with an extra -e but sounds the same.
items.ex: Mon père est ingénieur chez Renault.
items.exEn: My father is an engineer at Renault.

items.note: Feminine form of 'infirmier' (-er becomes -ère); a male nurse is 'un infirmier'.
Masculine -er ending; the feminine is 'la boulangère' with a grave accent that opens the vowel.
items.ex: Le boulanger fait du pain tous les matins.
items.exEn: The baker makes bread every morning.

items.note: The same word means avocado; context tells you which. Feminine: l'avocate.
items.ex: Mon frère est avocat à Paris.
items.exEn: My brother is a lawyer in Paris.

items.note: From 'vendre' (to sell); the feminine 'la vendeuse' follows the -eur / -euse pattern.
Masculine; feminine 'la patronne' doubles the -n and you finally hear it.
Literally 'in life'; 'Qu'est-ce que vous faites dans la vie ?' is the normal way to ask someone's job.
items.ex: Qu'est-ce que vous faites dans la vie ?
items.exEn: What do you do for a living?

teaching.rule: Days and months are written in lowercase in French: lundi, janvier. To say 'on Monday' (one time) just say the day on its own: 'Je travaille lundi'. To say 'on Mondays' (every week) add 'le': 'le lundi'. Months take 'en': en janvier, en juillet. Three seasons take 'en' (en été, en automne, en hiver) but spring takes 'au': au printemps.

examples.note: No word for 'on' and no article for a single day.
'en' + month, month in lowercase.

examples.en: In spring the weather is mild.
examples.note: Spring is the odd one out: 'au printemps', not 'en printemps'.

contrast.note: Among the seasons, only 'printemps' takes 'au'; été, automne and hiver take 'en'. This is a seasons-only quirk: months always take 'en' (en janvier, en mars).
'à + day' is a goodbye, not 'on Monday'; for 'on Monday' say just 'lundi'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers capitalise days and months and translate 'on Monday' as 'sur lundi' or 'à lundi'; write 'lundi' in lowercase and use it on its own.

probes.ex: Au printemps, les jardins sont pleins de fleurs.
probes.exEn: In spring the gardens are full of flowers.

probes.ex: Le dimanche, je fais la grasse matinée.

items.note: Lowercase in French; named after the moon (lune). On its own it means 'on Monday'.
items.ex: Je vais chez le médecin lundi.
items.exEn: I'm going to the doctor on Monday.

items.note: Lowercase; named after Mars, like 'Mardi gras' (Fat Tuesday).
items.ex: Le cours de français est mardi soir.
items.exEn: The French class is on Tuesday evening.

items.note: Lowercase; named after Mercury; in France many primary schools have a short day or no school on Wednesday.
items.ex: Les enfants n'ont pas école mercredi après-midi.
items.exEn: The children have no school on Wednesday afternoon.

items.note: Lowercase; named after Jupiter; the 'j' is soft, like the s in 'measure'.
items.exEn: I have an appointment on Thursday morning.

items.note: Lowercase; the -en- is a nasal sound, as in 'vent'.
items.ex: On va au cinéma vendredi soir.
items.exEn: We're going to the cinema on Friday evening.

items.note: Lowercase; from Latin 'sabbati dies'; 'le samedi' means every Saturday, e.g. market day.
items.ex: Il y a un marché samedi matin.
items.exEn: There's a market on Saturday morning.

items.note: Lowercase; 'le dimanche' with the article means every Sunday.
items.ex: Le dimanche, les magasins sont fermés.
items.exEn: On Sundays the shops are closed.

items.note: Borrowed from English but masculine and written with a hyphen; 'ce week-end' means this weekend.
items.ex: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
items.exEn: What are you doing this weekend?

items.note: Lowercase; months take 'en' for 'in': en janvier.
Lowercase; the -ll- is pronounced like a 'y' (zhwee-yeh); le 14 juillet is the national holiday.
items.ex: En juillet, beaucoup de Français sont en vacances.
items.exEn: In July many French people are on holiday.

items.note: Lowercase; dates go number + month with no 'of': le vingt-cinq décembre.
items.exEn: Christmas is on the twenty-fifth of December.

items.note: Masculine; the only season that takes 'au' (au printemps); the final -ps is silent.
Masculine (un été); 'in summer' is 'en été' with no article.
items.ex: En été, on va à la plage.
items.exEn: In summer we go to the beach.

items.note: Masculine (un automne); the -mn- is said like a single 'n' (oh-tonn).
Masculine (un hiver); silent h, so 'l'hiver' and 'en hiver' link the sounds.
items.ex: En hiver, les jours sont courts.
items.exEn: In winter the days are short.

teaching.rule: Adjectives are describing words like big, new or happy. In French they change their ending to match the noun they describe: add -e when the noun is feminine (grand → grande, petit → petite) and -s when it is plural. A handful of very common short adjectives (grand, petit, bon, mauvais, beau, nouveau, vieux, jeune) go BEFORE the noun; nearly every other adjective goes AFTER it, the opposite of English.

examples.note: maison is feminine, so grand takes an -e; the final d is now pronounced.
bon is one of the short adjectives that sit before the noun.
difficile is not in the short list, so it follows the noun; it already ends in -e, so the feminine looks the same.
beau becomes belle in the feminine and belles in the plural; des shrinks to de in front of a plural adjective.

contrast.fr: une voiture rouge (not une rouge voiture)
contrast.note: Colours and most other adjectives come after the noun; only the short beauty-age-goodness-size adjectives go first.

contrast.fr: Elle est grande. (not Elle est grand.)
contrast.note: Agreement also applies after être: the adjective matches the person being described, not just a noun next to it.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers put every adjective before the noun (une rouge voiture); only the short ones like grand, petit, bon, beau, nouveau and vieux go first, the rest follow the noun (une voiture rouge).

items.note: Means both big (for things) and tall (for people); goes before the noun and the feminine is grande with the d sounded.
Goes before the noun; the feminine petite makes the silent t audible (puh-TEET).
Goes before the noun; the feminine bonne doubles the n, and the vowel stops being nasal.
Goes before the noun; the final s is silent, and the feminine mauvaise makes it sound like z.
Goes before the noun; feminine belle, and bel before a masculine noun starting with a vowel (un bel homme).
Goes before the noun; feminine nouvelle, and nouvel before a masculine noun starting with a vowel (un nouvel ami).
Goes before the noun; feminine vieille, and vieil before a masculine noun starting with a vowel (un vieil homme).
Already ends in -e, so masculine and feminine look and sound the same; goes before the noun.
Adjectives ending in -eux swap to -euse in the feminine: heureuse; the final x is silent.
items.ex: Je suis heureux de vous voir.

items.note: Ends in -e, so one form for both genders; like most adjectives it goes after the noun (un exercice facile).
Ends in -e, so one form for both genders; goes after the noun (une question difficile).
Goes after the noun when it means expensive; the feminine is chère. Before a name it means 'dear' (Cher Paul).

teaching.rule: These are the verbs you will need in almost every conversation. The dictionary form (faire, voir, prendre) is the infinitive, the 'to ...' form; after je, tu, il and so on the ending changes (je fais, tu fais, il fait), and most of these verbs are irregular, so learn each one with its je form. The infinitive stays unchanged after vouloir, pouvoir and devoir: je veux manger, je peux venir, je dois partir.

examples.note: prendre (to take) is the normal verb for ordering food and drink; je prends is its je form.
pouvoir is conjugated (tu peux) and the second verb, venir, stays in the infinitive.
faire covers both 'do' and 'make'; tu fais is its tu form.

contrast.fr: Je veux un thé. (not Je vouloir un thé.)
contrast.note: The first verb after je must be conjugated; the infinitive is only used after another verb (je veux boire un thé).

contrast.fr: Je vois la tour Eiffel. (not Je regarde la tour Eiffel.)
contrast.note: voir is simply seeing with your eyes; regarder is watching or looking at something on purpose, so je regarde la tour Eiffel only if you are deliberately looking at it.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'je suis manger' for 'I am eating' because English uses 'to be' + -ing; French has no such form, so use the plain present: je mange.

items.note: One verb for both 'do' and 'make', and the base of many set phrases: faire la cuisine (cook), faire du sport; irregular (je fais, nous faisons, vous faites, ils font).
Irregular: je dis, tu dis, il dit, nous disons, vous dites, ils disent; French uses dire for both 'say' and 'tell'.
Seeing with your eyes (je vois, nous voyons, ils voient); to watch or look at on purpose you use regarder instead.
items.exEn: I want to see the sea.

items.note: Irregular (je viens, tu viens, il/elle vient, nous venons, ils viennent); venir de + place means 'to come from'.
Irregular (je prends, il prend, nous prenons, ils prennent); also the everyday verb for ordering: je prends un café.
Irregular (je veux, tu veux, il veut, nous voulons, ils veulent); je veux sounds blunt, so when ordering say je voudrais (I would like).
Irregular (je peux, tu peux, il peut, nous pouvons, ils peuvent); the next verb goes straight after it in the infinitive.
Irregular (je dois, tu dois, il doit, nous devons, ils doivent); followed directly by an infinitive, no 'to' needed.
A regular -er verb (je mange, tu manges, il/elle/on mange); on is the everyday spoken 'we' and takes the il form; nous mangeons keeps the e so the g stays soft.
Irregular: je bois, tu bois, il boit, but nous buvons, vous buvez, ils boivent.
An -er verb whose je, tu, il and ils forms take a grave accent: j'achète, tu achètes, il achète, ils achètent, but nous achetons, vous achetez.
items.exEn: I want to buy some bread.

items.note: Irregular (je lis, tu lis, il lit, nous lisons, ils lisent); do not confuse it with rire (to laugh), which differs only by the first sound.
items.exEn: She likes to read in the evening.

teaching.rule: The French R is made at the back of the throat, not with the tip of the tongue. Keep the tongue tip down behind your bottom teeth, raise the back of the tongue towards the soft palate and let the air rub through, like a very soft gargle or the 'ch' in Scottish 'loch'. It is strongest at the start of a word (rire), lighter between vowels (Paris) and almost whispered at the end of a word after a consonant (quatre).

examples.note: Two Rs: a clear one at the start, a softer one at the end; neither uses the tongue tip.
Between vowels the R is a light friction; the final s is silent (pa-REE).
After t at the end of a word the R is barely more than a breath: KATR.
