contrast.note: The English R curls the tongue tip back; the French one keeps it down and makes the sound in the throat.
For L the tongue tip touches the ridge behind the teeth; for R it stays down, so the two words must sound clearly different.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers curl the tongue tip back for an American-style R (as in 'red'); keep the tip down and make the friction at the back of the throat instead, and do not roll it like Spanish either.

probes.exEn: We are going to the sea.

items.note: Start with the tongue tip down and the back of the tongue raised; the first R is strong, the final one soft. Keep it distinct from lire (to read).
Word-initial R before 'i': make the throat friction first, then slide into a tight 'ee'; the z is silent (REE).
Final R after a vowel is fully pronounced: finish the word with a short throat rub. It sounds exactly like mère (mother) and maire (mayor).
items.exEn: We are going to the sea.

items.note: After t the R is a quick, light scrape rather than a full sound; the final s is silent (TREH).
Consonant + R at the end of a word: the R is almost whispered and the final -e is silent, so it sounds like KATR.
The 'vr' cluster: keep the lips touching the teeth for v and let the throat R follow immediately, with no vowel in between (VREH).
Double rr is the same single throat sound, never a roll; the final -er sounds like 'ay' with no R at all (a-ree-VAY).
items.exEn: The train is about to arrive.

items.note: The 'fr' cluster: f then straight into the throat R, and the vowel after it is nasal (FRAHNSS).
R between two vowels is light and quick: bu-RO, with rounded lips for both vowels; also means desk.
Word-initial R before the rounded 'oo' vowel: round your lips while the throat friction is still going (ROOT).
Word-initial R before 'a': open the mouth wide right after the throat friction (ra-PEED); same form for masculine and feminine.
R at the start before an open 'eh' (the ê) and a v at the end: REHV; the final -e is silent.

teaching.rule: A nasal vowel is a vowel where the air comes out through your nose and mouth at the same time, and the n or m written after it is NOT pronounced as a separate sound. French has three main ones: 'on' as in bon (lips rounded), 'an/en' as in cent (mouth wide open) and 'in/ain/ein/un' as in vin (lips slightly spread, like a nasal 'eh'). Look for a vowel + n or m at the end of a word or before another consonant; when the n or m is followed by a vowel (bonne, une, voisine), the vowel is normal and you hear the n.

examples.note: Say 'oh' with rounded lips and let the air go through your nose; do not close your mouth for an n at the end.
Open your mouth wide as for 'ah' and let the air go through your nose; 'en' and 'an' spell the same sound.
Spread your lips slightly as for 'eh' and send the air through your nose; 'in', 'ain', 'ein' and 'un' all spell this sound in everyday Paris French.

contrast.note: In bon the vowel is nasal and there is no n sound; in bonne the n is followed by a vowel, so the vowel is plain 'o' and the n is pronounced.
Three different words that differ only by which nasal vowel you make: spread lips (vin), open mouth (vent), rounded lips (vont).

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers finish the word with an English n or ng (saying 'bon' like 'bonn'); the tongue must not touch the roof of the mouth at the end, the nasal sound is in the vowel itself.

items.note: The 'on' nasal: round your lips as for 'oh' and let the air out through your nose; the written n is silent (NOH with nasal resonance).
'on' before a consonant is nasal; the final t is silent, so pont sounds just like the nasal vowel after p (POH).
A written m after the vowel works exactly like n: nom and non sound identical, both ending in the nasal 'on' with no closed lips.
'on' + d: make the rounded nasal vowel, then the d; tout le monde (literally 'all the world') means everybody.
The 'an/en' nasal: drop your jaw as for 'ah' and send the air through your nose; the final t is silent (LAH with nasal resonance).
'an' before g is the same open nasal as in lent; langue also means tongue, the body part.
items.ex: Le français est une belle langue.

items.note: 'en' before d gives the open nasal (a-TAHNDR); a false friend, since attendre means to wait, not to attend.
items.exEn: I am going to wait here.

items.note: Two different nasals in one word: open-mouth 'an' first, then rounded-lips 'on' (shah-SOH), with no n sound in either.
The 'in' nasal: spread your lips slightly as for 'eh' and send the air through your nose (ma-TEH); the n is not pronounced.
'ain' is spelled differently but is the same nasal as 'in' (TREH with nasal resonance); en retard has the open 'en' nasal.
'in' at the end of the word is nasal: vwa-ZEH with the air through the nose and no n sound at all.
Add -e and the n is now followed by a vowel, so the nasal disappears: vwa-ZEEN with a clear n; the same switch happens in bon/bonne and un/une.

teaching.rule: Always open any exchange with bonjour (bonsoir after about 6 pm) before you ask for anything, even in a shop or at a ticket window, and close it with au revoir; skipping these sounds rude in France. Add s'il vous plaît when you ask for something and merci when you get it, and answer merci with de rien. Keep salut and s'il te plaît for friends and people you call tu.

examples.fr: Bonjour, un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
examples.note: Greeting first, then the request, then s'il vous plaît at the end: the standard shop formula.

examples.en: Thank you very much! — You're welcome.
examples.note: de rien (literally 'of nothing') is the everyday reply to thanks.
Leaving a shop: au revoir plus a wish like bonne journée (daytime) or bonne soirée (evening).
salut is only for friends and family; it also works as 'bye'.

contrast.note: salut with a stranger, a shopkeeper or your boss sounds overly familiar; use bonjour with anyone you would call vous.
bonne nuit is only said when someone is going to bed; to greet people in the evening use bonsoir.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers walk up to a counter and start with their request, as they would at home; in France say bonjour first, otherwise the person may not respond warmly or at all.

probes.exEn: Excuse me, do you have the time?

items.note: The default daytime greeting, said to everyone before anything else, from shopkeepers to bus drivers; used until early evening, and normally only once a day to the same person.
items.ex: Bonjour, vous avez une table pour deux ?
items.exEn: Hello, do you have a table for two?

items.note: Replaces bonjour from about 6 pm; used both when arriving and, more formally, when leaving in the evening.
items.ex: Bonsoir, je voudrais réserver une table.
items.exEn: Good evening, I would like to book a table.

items.note: Casual greeting for friends, family and classmates, and also a casual goodbye; never use it with a stranger or someone you call vous.
Used constantly, even for tiny things like being handed change; to refuse an offer politely say non merci.
Literally 'if it pleases you', with the polite vous; add it at the end of any request to a stranger, waiter or shop assistant.
The same formula with te, for one person you call tu: a friend, a family member or a child.
items.ex: Papa, passe-moi le sel, s'il te plaît.
items.exEn: Dad, pass me the salt, please.

items.note: Literally 'of nothing'; the relaxed, everyday reply to merci in any situation.
A more formal reply to thanks than de rien, typical from staff or with vous; it also means 'please, go ahead' when you hold a door or offer a seat.
items.ex: — Merci beaucoup, madame. — Je vous en prie.
items.exEn: — Thank you very much, madam. — You're welcome.

items.note: To get a stranger's or a waiter's attention, or to squeeze past someone; uses the vous form, so with a friend say excuse-moi.
items.exEn: Excuse me, where are the toilets?

items.note: Literally 'until seeing again'; the standard goodbye in any situation, said every time you leave a shop or office.
items.exEn: Goodbye and have a good day!

items.note: Literally 'delighted', said when you are introduced to someone; a woman says and writes enchantée.
items.exEn: Nice to meet you, my name is Paul.

items.note: A quick apology when you bump into someone, or, with rising voice, a request to repeat; for a real apology use désolé (désolée for a woman).

teaching.rule: French has two words for 'you'. Use tu when you talk to ONE person you are close to: a friend, a family member, a child, a classmate. Use vous with one person you don't know well, someone older, or anyone serving you or working with you (shopkeeper, waiter, boss), and ALWAYS when you talk to two or more people. The verb changes with it: tu takes an -s ending (tu parles, tu as), vous takes -ez (vous parlez, vous avez; the one exception to learn is vous êtes). When in doubt, say vous: it is never rude, and the other person will offer 'tu' if they want it.

examples.en: Are you coming tonight? (to a friend)
examples.note: One close person, so tu; the verb ends in -s (viens).

examples.fr: Vous avez une table pour deux ?
examples.en: Do you have a table for two? (to a waiter)
examples.note: A stranger doing their job gets vous; the verb ends in -ez (avez).
Even children get vous when there are several of them: vous is the only plural 'you'.

examples.en: Can we use 'tu' with each other?
examples.note: The polite way to switch; wait for the older or more senior person to suggest it.

contrast.en: Hello madam, do you have the time? (wrong register)
contrast.note: Madame signals a stranger, so tu sounds rude here; say 'vous avez l'heure ?'.

contrast.en: Hi Léa, how are you? (too stiff)
contrast.note: Salut and a first name are informal, so vous is odd here; say 'tu vas bien ?'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers default to tu because it feels like plain 'you'; default to vous with anyone you would not call by their first name, and remember that a group is always vous.

probes.en: you (formal, or more than one person)

probes.exEn: Excuse me, do you have the time?

items.note: The verb for formal address, a regular -er verb built on vous (je vouvoie, tu vouvoies, il vouvoie); it is what you do with strangers, elders and colleagues you don't know well.
items.exEn: I always address my boss as 'vous'.

items.note: The verb for informal address, built on tu; used with friends, family and children.
items.ex: Tu peux me tutoyer, tu sais.
items.exEn: You can call me 'tu', you know.

items.note: The standard phrase for proposing the switch to informal; the senior or older person usually says it first.
items.ex: On se tutoie ? — Oui, bien sûr !
items.exEn: Shall we use 'tu'? — Yes, of course!

items.note: Masculine noun for the habit of saying vous; it is the normal register at work and in shops.
items.ex: Le vouvoiement est normal au travail.

items.en: Where do you live? (to a friend)
items.note: Informal question: tu plus the -s verb ending (habites), with the question word at the end as in casual speech.
items.ex: Tu habites où ? Moi, à Lyon.
items.exEn: Where do you live? Me, in Lyon.

items.en: Where do you live? (to a stranger)
items.note: Same question in the polite register: vous plus the -ez ending (habitez).
items.exEn: And you, where do you live?

items.en: Do you have the time? (to a friend)
items.note: Casual request to a peer: tu and the short verb form 'as'; note the rising question tone with no 'est-ce que'.
items.ex: Tu as l'heure ? Mon portable est mort.
items.exEn: Do you have the time? My phone is dead.

items.en: Do you have the time? (to a stranger)
items.note: The vous version of the same request, usually opened with 'excusez-moi' when speaking to someone in the street.
items.exEn: Excuse me, do you have the time?

items.en: Can you help me? (to a stranger)
items.note: Polite request with the verb before vous and a hyphen; the -ez ending (pouvez) marks the formal register.

items.en: Can you help me? (to a friend)
items.note: Informal request: tu and the -x ending of 'peux' (pouvoir keeps -x instead of -s in the tu form).
items.exEn: Can you help me? It's heavy.

items.en: What would you like? (shop or café)
items.note: The stock phrase a server or shopkeeper uses to a customer; the customer is always vous, so answer with vous too.
Vous for a group: prêts takes plural -s because it describes several people, even if they are all close friends.
items.ex: Allez, vous êtes prêts ? On part !
items.exEn: Come on, are you all ready? We're leaving!

teaching.rule: A French adjective changes its ending to match the noun it describes, whether it sits next to the noun or after être (to be). Start from the masculine form: add -e for a feminine noun (petit / petite), add -s for a plural (petit / petits; if the masculine already ends in -s or -x, like français or heureux, the plural adds nothing), and add -es for feminine plural (petites). If the masculine already ends in -e (rouge, calme), it stays the same for feminine. Listen for the difference: adding -e often makes a silent final consonant audible (petit 'peu-ti' becomes petite 'peu-tit').

examples.fr: un petit café, une petite maison
examples.en: a small cafe, a small house
examples.note: maison is feminine, so petit takes -e; you now hear the t at the end of petite.
Plural noun, so content takes -s, even though the adjective sits after être and the -s is silent.
Feminine plural: both endings stack, grand + e + s = grandes.

examples.fr: un pull rouge, une jupe rouge
examples.en: a red sweater, a red skirt
examples.note: rouge already ends in -e, so masculine and feminine look and sound the same.

contrast.note: Adjectives in -eux do not just add -e: -eux becomes -euse (heureux / heureuse). 'heureuxe' does not exist.
beau is irregular: its feminine is belle, not 'beaue'. Learn beau / belle, nouveau / nouvelle, vieux / vieille as pairs.
A mixed group takes the masculine plural: contents, not contentes, even with one man among many women.

teaching.commonMistake: English adjectives never change, so learners write 'une grand maison' or 'elles sont fatigué'; always check the noun's gender and number and adjust the ending (grande, fatiguées).

probes.ex: Ma voisine a une voiture verte.
probes.exEn: My neighbour has a green car.

probes.ex: Ils sont fatigués après le travail.

items.note: Feminine of petit: add -e, and the final t, silent in petit, is now pronounced ('peu-tit').
After être the adjective still agrees with the subject: elle is feminine, so grand takes -e and you hear the d. For people grand means tall; for things it means big.
Plural masculine: add -s to grand. The -s is silent, so grand and grands sound identical; only the article and verb show the plural.
Feminine plural stacks both endings: vert + e + s = vertes; pommes is feminine and plural.
calme already ends in -e, so it does not change for a feminine noun; only the plural adds -s (calmes).
Adjectives in -eux change to -euse for the feminine: heureux / heureuse. Listen for the new 'z' sound at the end.
Adjectives in -f change to -ve for the feminine: neuf / neuve; voiture is feminine.
beau is irregular: the feminine is belle, with a double l; maison is feminine.
blanc is irregular: the feminine is blanche, and the silent c turns into an audible 'sh' sound.
items.exEn: She is wearing a white shirt.

items.note: bon doubles the n before adding -e: bonne. The nasal 'bon' becomes a clear 'bon-n' sound.
fatigué keeps its accent and adds -s for a plural subject; a group with at least one man uses this masculine plural form.
Nationality adjectives agree too and are written with a small letter: français + e + s = françaises for a group of women.

teaching.rule: In French most adjectives come AFTER the noun, the opposite of English: une voiture rouge (a red car), un film français. A small group of very common short adjectives come BEFORE the noun, as in English; remember them with BAGS: Beauty (beau, joli), Age (jeune, vieux, nouveau), Goodness (bon, mauvais), Size (grand, petit, gros). Colours and nationalities always go after. Wherever it sits, the adjective still agrees with the noun.

examples.note: Colour adjectives always follow the noun: say 'a shirt blue'.
petit is a Size adjective (BAGS), so it goes before the noun, as in English.
vieux is an Age adjective, so it comes first; it also takes the irregular feminine vieille.
Nationality adjectives follow the noun and are written with a small letter.

contrast.fr: un ancien collègue / un immeuble ancien
contrast.en: a former colleague / an old building
contrast.note: A few adjectives change meaning with position: ancien before the noun means 'former', after it means 'old'.
nouveau, beau and vieux take a special form (nouvel, bel, vieil) before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or silent h, precisely because they come first.
Long adjectives (intéressant, important, difficile) go after the noun even when English puts them first.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers put every adjective before the noun ('une rouge voiture', 'un français film'); keep the English order only for the short BAGS adjectives and put everything else after the noun.

probes.en: correct: colour adjectives go after the noun
probes.ex: Elle a acheté une voiture rouge.
options: wrong: it should be une rouge voiture
correct: rouge is a BAGS adjective, so it can go anywhere
wrong: it should be une voiture rouges

probes.en: correct: vieux is an Age adjective (BAGS), so it goes before the noun
probes.ex: Un vieil homme attend le bus.
probes.exEn: An old man is waiting for the bus.
options: wrong: it should be un homme vieil
wrong: it should be un homme vieux
correct: every French adjective goes before the noun

probes.ex: Marc est un ancien ami de ma mère.
probes.exEn: Marc is a former friend of my mother's.

items.note: Default order: noun first, then the adjective. Colours always follow the noun; rouge already ends in -e so it does not change.
items.ex: Mon père a une voiture rouge.
items.exEn: My father has a red car.

items.note: beau is a Beauty adjective (BAGS), so it goes before the noun, as in English.
grand is a Size adjective, so it comes before the noun, and takes -e because maison is feminine.
items.ex: Nous habitons dans une grande maison.
items.exEn: We live in a big house.

items.note: petit (Size) goes before the noun; problème is masculine despite ending in -e, so no agreement change.
bon (Goodness) goes before the noun; its opposite mauvais does the same: un mauvais livre.
nouveau (Age: newness) goes first, and takes the irregular feminine nouvelle because idée is feminine.
vieux (Age) goes before the noun and becomes vieil before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or silent h, to avoid two vowels clashing.
items.ex: Je parle avec un vieil homme.
items.exEn: I'm talking with an old man.

items.note: jeune (Age) comes before the noun; it already ends in -e, so it is the same for masculine and feminine.
items.ex: Une jeune femme attend le bus.
items.exEn: A young woman is waiting for the bus.

items.note: Colour after the noun, and bleu takes -e to agree with the feminine robe.
items.exEn: She is wearing a blue dress.

items.note: Nationality adjectives always follow the noun and take a small letter, unlike English 'French'.
items.ex: On regarde un film français ce soir.
items.exEn: We're watching a French film tonight.

items.note: ancien before the noun means 'former, previous'; the position changes the meaning, not just the style.
items.ex: C'est un ancien ami de mon père.
items.exEn: He's a former friend of my father's.

items.note: ancien after the noun means 'old, historic'; compare un ancien ami (a former friend). Feminine maison gives ancienne with a double n.
items.ex: Ils habitent dans une maison ancienne.
items.exEn: They live in an old house.

teaching.rule: When you talk about SOME of something you cannot count (bread, water, music, time), French needs a small word before the noun where English can leave a gap: je mange du pain (I eat bread). Pick it by the noun's gender: du for masculine (du pain), de la for feminine (de la soupe), de l' before a vowel or silent h (de l'eau), and des for plurals (des fruits). After a negative (ne... pas, except after être: ce n'est pas du pain) and after quantity words (beaucoup, un peu, trop) all of these shrink to plain de: pas de pain, beaucoup de pain.

examples.note: pain is masculine, so 'some' is du (a contraction of de + le).
limonade is feminine, so 'some' is de la; English drops the word, French cannot.
Before a vowel de la and du both become de l'.

examples.fr: Je ne mange pas de viande.
examples.note: After ne... pas the partitive collapses to de: not 'pas de la viande'.

contrast.note: After aimer, adorer, détester and préférer use le / la / les (bread in general), not du: you like the whole category, not a portion.
un pain is one countable loaf; du pain is an unmeasured amount. Same noun, different article.
After a quantity word there is no article at all: beaucoup de, never 'beaucoup du'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers drop the article ('je mange pain', 'je bois eau') because English says 'I eat bread'; French always needs du / de la / de l' / des before an uncounted noun.

probes.ex: Il reste de la soupe dans la casserole.
probes.exEn: There is some soup left in the pan.

probes.fr: Je ne bois pas de lait.
probes.ex: Je ne bois pas de lait le matin.
probes.exEn: I don't drink milk in the morning.
options: I drink a lot of milk.

probes.en: some water (noun starts with a vowel)
probes.ex: Je bois de l'eau à chaque repas.
probes.exEn: I drink water at every meal.

items.note: pain is masculine, so 'some' is du, a contraction of de + le; French cannot drop the article the way English does.
items.ex: Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît.

items.note: soupe is feminine, so 'some' is de la, written as two words and never contracted.
items.ex: Ce soir, je mange de la soupe.

items.note: eau starts with a vowel, so de la becomes de l' with an apostrophe, whatever the gender.
argent is masculine but starts with a vowel, so du becomes de l'; money is uncountable, hence the partitive.
items.ex: Tu as de l'argent sur toi ?
items.exEn: Do you have any money on you?

items.note: fromage is masculine (most -age nouns are), so du; English 'there is cheese' has no article, French must add one.
items.ex: Il y a du fromage dans le frigo.
items.exEn: There is cheese in the fridge.

items.note: confiture is feminine, so de la; you spread an amount of it, not one whole jam, so the partitive fits.
items.ex: Elle met de la confiture sur sa tartine.
items.exEn: She puts jam on her toast.

items.note: For plurals the 'some' word is des; French counts fruits in the plural where English says 'fruit'.
items.exEn: I'm buying fruit at the market.

items.note: After ne... pas every partitive shrinks to plain de: pas de sucre, never 'pas du sucre'.
items.ex: Je ne prends pas de sucre dans mon café.
items.exEn: I don't take sugar in my coffee.

items.note: After a quantity word (un peu, beaucoup, trop, assez) there is no article: just de + noun.
items.ex: Je mets un peu de lait dans mon thé.
items.exEn: I put a little milk in my tea.

items.note: Quantity word + plain de, whatever the gender or number of the noun that follows; 'beaucoup du' is wrong.
items.ex: Nous avons beaucoup de travail cette semaine.
items.exEn: We have a lot of work this week.

items.note: Activities use faire + partitive: faire du sport, faire de la natation, faire du piano. sport is masculine, so du.
items.ex: J'aime faire du sport le week-end.
items.exEn: I like doing sport at the weekend.

items.note: Abstract uncountables (music, patience, luck) take the partitive too; musique is feminine, so de la.
items.ex: J'écoute de la musique dans le bus.
items.exEn: I listen to music on the bus.

teaching.rule: To say what is about to happen or what you plan to do, French uses aller (to go) in the present plus the verb in its dictionary form (the infinitive, ending in -er, -ir or -re), exactly like English 'I am going to eat': je vais manger. Only aller changes with the person (je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont); the second verb never changes. To say something is NOT going to happen, wrap ne... pas around the aller part: je ne vais pas sortir. This is the everyday future in spoken French, so listen for vais / vas / va followed straight by another verb.

examples.note: vais (I go) + manger in its dictionary form: nothing else to conjugate.
Weather and predictions use the same pattern: va + infinitive.

examples.en: We're going to visit the museum.
examples.note: Only allons carries the person; visiter stays unchanged.

examples.fr: Je ne vais pas sortir ce soir.
examples.en: I'm not going to go out tonight.
examples.note: ne and pas surround vais, not the infinitive: 'je vais ne pas sortir' is wrong.

contrast.note: aller followed by a place (not a verb) is simple movement, not a future: to Paris is à Paris.
The plain present says what happens habitually; je vais manger says it is about to happen.
The verb after aller must be the dictionary form (manger), never a past participle (mangé) or a conjugated form (mange).

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers conjugate both verbs ('je vais mange') or drop aller and use the present for plans; keep aller conjugated and leave the second verb in its dictionary form: je vais manger.

probes.ex: Nous allons partir à huit heures.
probes.exEn: We're going to leave at eight.

probes.ex: Prends un parapluie, il va pleuvoir.
probes.exEn: Take an umbrella, it's going to rain.

probes.ex: Désolé, je ne vais pas venir ce soir.
probes.exEn: Sorry, I'm not going to come tonight.

items.note: vais is the je form of aller; the verb after it stays in its dictionary form (manger), whoever the subject is.
items.ex: Ce midi, je vais manger au restaurant.
items.exEn: At lunchtime I'm going to eat at the restaurant.

items.note: Same pattern with partir: vais + dictionary form; there is no need to learn a future tense for this.
vas is the tu form of aller; the final s is silent, so vais and vas sound almost the same, and the subject tells them apart.
Weather uses il as a dummy subject, then va + dictionary form; pleuvoir only ever appears in the il form.
allons is the nous form of aller (the s of nous links: 'nou-za-lon'); visiter stays unchanged.
items.exEn: We're going to visit Paris tomorrow.

items.note: allez is the vous form; a favourite phrase of French shopkeepers and waiters when recommending something.
items.exEn: You're going to love this film.

items.note: vont is the irregular ils form of aller; arriver stays in the dictionary form.
items.ex: Ils vont arriver dans dix minutes.
items.exEn: They're going to arrive in ten minutes.

items.en: I'm not going to go out
items.note: To negate, ne... pas wraps around the aller part only; the second verb sits outside, after pas.
items.ex: Je ne vais pas sortir ce soir.
items.exEn: I'm not going to go out tonight.

items.note: Time markers like ce soir, demain, ce week-end, bientôt usually accompany the near future to say when.
items.ex: Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire ce soir ?
items.exEn: What are you going to do tonight?

items.en: let's get going (literally: we are going to go there)
items.note: on (we, informal) + va + y aller (go there); a very common spoken phrase to announce leaving.

items.en: what are you going to do?
items.note: In casual speech the question word quoi stays at the end; the standard version is Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire ?
items.ex: Et toi, tu vas faire quoi ce week-end ?
items.exEn: And you, what are you going to do this weekend?

items.note: A reassuring set phrase: ça (it) + va + aller; literally 'it is going to go'.
items.ex: Ne t'inquiète pas, ça va aller.

teaching.rule: A reflexive verb is one where the action comes back onto the person doing it: se laver (to wash oneself), se lever (to get oneself up). In the dictionary it starts with se; in a sentence you swap se for a little pronoun that matches the subject: je me, tu te, il/elle/on se, nous nous, vous vous, ils/elles se. The pronoun sits right before the verb, and before a vowel me/te/se shrink to m'/t'/s' (je m'appelle). Many daily-routine verbs are reflexive in French even when English has no 'myself': getting up, going to bed, getting dressed, hurrying, having fun. In the negative, ne goes before the pronoun and pas after the verb: je ne me lève pas.

examples.fr: Je me lève à sept heures.
examples.note: se lever becomes me lève after je: the pronoun matches the subject.
With tu the pronoun is te, and the verb takes its usual tu ending -es.
se shrinks to s' before the vowel of appelle.
nous appears twice: once as subject, once as the reflexive pronoun; this is normal, not a typo.

examples.fr: Je ne me lève pas tôt.
examples.note: ne... pas wraps both the pronoun and the verb together.

contrast.note: NOT 'Je lave' on its own, which means you wash something else, like the car.
NOT 'Elle se habille': se must shrink to s' before a vowel.
NOT 'Je repose': French treats resting as something you do to yourself, so the pronoun is compulsory.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers drop the reflexive pronoun ('Je lève à sept heures') because English has no 'myself' there; always keep the matching pronoun before the verb (Je me lève).

probes.ex: Je me lève à sept heures.
Nous nous couchons tard le samedi.
probes.exEn: We go to bed late on Saturdays.

items.note: The pronoun tells you the washing lands on the subject; after je it becomes me lave.
Literally 'to raise oneself'; the e of lever turns into è (lève) whenever the ending after it is silent: je me lève, but nous nous levons.
items.ex: Je me lève à sept heures.

items.note: French says 'I call myself' for names; m' replaces me because appelle starts with a vowel.
With il the pronoun stays se; coucher alone means to put someone else to bed.
Resting is reflexive in French; on takes se like il and elle.
Always reflexive; the command form drops the subject and puts toi after the verb: Dépêche-toi !
items.ex: Il se dépêche pour prendre le train.
items.exEn: He's hurrying to catch the train.

items.note: Literally 'to amuse oneself'; s' because amuser starts with a vowel, and ils takes the same se/s' as il.
items.ex: Les enfants s'amusent dans le jardin.
items.exEn: The children are having fun in the garden.

items.note: Waking up is reflexive; réveiller without the pronoun means to wake someone else.
items.ex: Je me réveille à six heures.

items.note: The h of habiller is silent, so se shrinks to s' just as before a vowel.
items.exEn: She gets dressed quickly in the morning.

items.note: French uses the reflexive pronoun plus les dents instead of 'my/your teeth'; the pronoun already says whose.
The first nous is the subject, the second is the reflexive pronoun; saying nous only once is a mistake.
items.ex: Le samedi, nous nous levons tard.
items.exEn: On Saturdays we get up late.

items.note: In the negative, ne comes before the pronoun and pas after the verb, so the pronoun stays glued to the verb.
items.ex: Le dimanche, je ne me lève pas tôt.
items.exEn: On Sundays I don't get up early.

teaching.rule: Use the passé composé to say something happened and is over: 'I ate', 'she finished', 'we saw'. Build it from two words: the present tense of avoir (j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont) plus a fixed form of the verb called the past participle. To make the participle, cut the ending off the dictionary form and add -é for -er verbs (manger → mangé), -i for -ir verbs (finir → fini), -u for -re verbs (vendre → vendu). A handful of very common verbs have irregular participles you simply learn: fait, eu, vu, pris, été, compris. Listen for the little avoir word right before the verb; that is the signal you are hearing the past.

examples.note: j'ai (present of avoir) + mangé (manger with -er replaced by -é).
finir is an -ir verb, so its participle ends in -i: fini.
vendre is an -re verb, so its participle ends in -u: vendu.
prendre is irregular: the participle is pris, not 'prendu'.
The negative ne... pas wraps around the avoir word only; the participle stays outside.

contrast.note: NOT 'Je mangé': French needs the helper avoir; the participle alone is not a sentence.
NOT 'Elle est été': the verb être itself uses avoir in the past, with the participle été.
NOT 'Je vois un film hier': a finished action with 'yesterday' needs the past, not the present.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers drop the helper verb and say 'Je mangé' or 'Je vu'; always put the present of avoir first (J'ai mangé, J'ai vu), then the participle.

probes.ex: J'ai mangé une pizza hier soir.
probes.exEn: I ate a pizza last night.

probes.ex: Il a fini son travail à midi.
probes.exEn: He finished his work at noon.

probes.ex: J'ai pris le train ce matin.
probes.exEn: I took the train this morning.

items.note: j'ai is the present of avoir; mangé is manger with its -er ending swapped for -é, the pattern for all regular -er verbs.
items.ex: Hier soir, j'ai mangé une pizza.
items.exEn: Last night I ate a pizza.

items.note: tu as is the tu form of avoir; parlé follows the -er → -é pattern and never changes for the subject.
finir is an -ir verb, so the participle drops -ir and adds -i: fini.
vendre is an -re verb, so the participle drops -re and adds -u: vendu.
vous avez is the vous form of avoir; visité is another regular -er participle, the same whether vous is one polite person or a group.
faire is irregular: its participle is fait, so it covers both 'did' and 'made'.
items.ex: J'ai fait du sport ce matin.
items.exEn: I did some exercise this morning.

items.note: avoir is its own helper here: j'ai + eu, the tiny irregular participle of avoir, pronounced like the u in 'tu'.
items.exEn: I was lucky. (literally: I had luck)

items.note: voir is irregular: the participle is vu, one syllable, not 'voiré'.
prendre is irregular: the participle is pris; the same form works for its cousins appris (learned) and compris (understood).
Surprisingly, être takes avoir in the past: elle a + été, and été never changes to match the subject.
items.ex: Elle a été malade toute la semaine.

items.note: The negative wraps only the helper: n'ai pas, then the participle compris (from comprendre) sits after it.
A time word that signals a finished action, so the verb next to it goes into the passé composé, not the present.

teaching.rule: A small group of verbs about coming, going and changing state (aller, venir, revenir, partir, arriver, entrer, rentrer, sortir, monter, descendre, rester, tomber, naître, mourir, devenir, and all reflexive verbs, the ones with me/te/se before the verb, like se lever) build their past with être instead of avoir: je suis allé, elle est partie. With être, the participle behaves like an adjective and must match the subject: add -e for a woman or girl (allée), -s for a group (allés), -es for a group of women (allées). The extra letters are silent, so you see the difference only in writing. When you hear suis, es, est, sommes, êtes or sont before a participle, you are in this group.

examples.note: aller takes être (je suis); a male speaker writes allé.

examples.fr: Elle est allée à la plage.
examples.note: Same verb, female subject: allée gets a silent -e to match elle.

examples.fr: Nous sommes partis à huit heures.
examples.note: nous is a group, so partis takes -s; if everyone in the group is female, parties.
Every reflexive verb (se lever, se coucher...) takes être: me suis + levé.
The negative wraps être (ne suis pas); the participle follows outside.

contrast.note: NOT 'Elle a arrivé': arriver is a movement verb, so it needs être, and the participle agrees (arrivée).
NOT 'Il a venu': venir belongs to the être group; venu, not 'veni'.
NOT 'Je suis mangé': manger is not a movement or reflexive verb, so it stays with avoir.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers use avoir for every verb ('J'ai allé'); with movement, state-change and reflexive verbs switch to être (Je suis allé) and add -e / -s to the participle to match who did it.

probes.ex: Elle est allée à Paris hier.
Marie est partie à huit heures.
Nous sommes rentrés tard hier soir.
probes.exEn: We came home late last night.

items.note: aller takes être (je suis) and allé matches the subject: a female speaker writes allée, sounding exactly the same.
Because elle is feminine, the participle takes a silent -e: allée; the -e shows only in writing.
items.ex: Elle est allée à la plage.

items.note: partir takes être, and a group adds -s: partis (parties for an all-female group).
items.ex: Nous sommes partis à huit heures.

items.note: venir is irregular (venu, not 'veni') and takes être; il is masculine singular, so no extra letter.
items.ex: Il est venu avec sa sœur.

items.note: arriver looks like a normal -er verb but it describes movement, so it takes être and agrees: arrivée for elle.
naître (to be born) is a change of state, so être + né; a woman writes née.
rentrer (to go back home) takes être; ils is plural, so rentrés ends in -s.
items.ex: Ils sont rentrés tard hier soir.
items.exEn: They came home late last night.

items.note: sortir takes être (tu es); write sortie if you are talking to a woman, same sound.
items.exEn: Did you go out last night?

items.note: monter takes être; elles is feminine plural, so the participle gets both -e and -s: montées.
items.ex: Elles sont montées au premier étage.
items.exEn: They (the women) went up to the first floor.

items.note: tomber (to fall) is in the être group even though it is not really 'going' anywhere; learn it with the movement verbs.
items.ex: Il est tombé dans la rue.

items.note: All reflexive verbs take être: the reflexive pronoun me comes first, then suis, then the participle (levée for a woman).
items.ex: Je me suis levé à six heures.

items.note: rester (to stay) takes être; ne... pas wraps suis only, and the participle resté (restée for a woman) comes after pas.
items.ex: Je ne suis pas resté longtemps.

teaching.rule: The French word for 'in' or 'to' depends on what kind of place follows. Before a city use à (à Paris). Before a country it depends on the country's gender: en for feminine countries, which are nearly all those ending in -e (en France), au for masculine ones (au Canada), aux for plural ones (aux États-Unis). For someone's home or a professional's office use chez plus the person (chez moi, chez le médecin). To say where you come from, use de (je viens de Paris, de France), which fuses with le/les into du / des (du Canada, des États-Unis). For time: à for clock times (à midi), en for months and most seasons (en juillet), but au printemps for spring. Use depuis when something started in the past and is still going on, pendant for a finished stretch, dans for 'in X minutes from now', and jusqu'à for 'until'.

examples.note: Cities always take à, whatever their size or spelling.
France ends in -e, so it is feminine and takes en.
Canada does not end in -e, so it is masculine and takes au (à + le fused).
Clock times take à, like English 'at'.

examples.en: I've lived here for two years.
examples.note: The living started two years ago and continues now, so depuis with a present-tense verb.

contrast.note: NOT 'Je vais en Lyon': en is for feminine countries, never for cities.
NOT 'dans juillet': dans means 'inside' or 'X time from now', not 'in a month'.
NOT 'depuis le film': the sleeping is over, so pendant, not depuis.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers use one word for every 'in' ('dans Paris', 'dans France'); pick à for cities, en / au / aux for countries by gender, and keep dans for physical 'inside'.

probes.ex: J'habite à Paris depuis dix ans.
probes.exEn: I've lived in Paris for ten years.

probes.ex: Elle est en France pour le travail.
probes.exEn: She is in France for work.

probes.ex: J'apprends le français depuis un an.
probes.exEn: I've been learning French for a year.

items.note: A city takes à for both 'in' and 'to'; the accent on à is what separates it from a (has).
France ends in -e, so it is feminine and takes en with no article; the same works for en Espagne, en Italie.
Canada is masculine (no final -e), so à + le fuses into au; likewise au Japon, au Portugal.
États-Unis is plural, so à + les fuses into aux; the x links to the vowel: o-zé-ta-zu-ni.
items.exEn: They live in the United States.

items.note: chez means 'at the home of' and is followed by a person or pronoun, never by a building word.
items.ex: On dîne chez moi ce soir.
items.exEn: We're having dinner at my place tonight.

items.note: de says where something or someone comes from; with a masculine or plural country it fuses: du Canada, des États-Unis, but de France.
Clock times take à: à midi, à huit heures, à minuit.
Months take en, with no article and a lowercase month name.
For the seasons, en goes with the three that start with a vowel (en été, en automne, en hiver) and au with printemps; months always take en, whatever letter they start with.
The action started in the past and is still true now, so French uses the present tense with depuis where English says 'have been'.
items.exEn: I've lived here for two years.

items.note: A stretch of time that is finished or clearly bounded; it goes with the past tense, unlike depuis.
With a length of time, dans means 'after that much time has passed', a false friend of 'inside'.
items.ex: Le film commence dans une heure.
items.exEn: The film starts in an hour.

items.note: jusque + à fuse with an apostrophe; before le it becomes jusqu'au (jusqu'au soir).
items.ex: Le magasin est ouvert jusqu'à vingt heures.
items.exEn: The shop is open until 8 pm.

teaching.rule: Many French words end in a written consonant that is normally silent (vous, les, petit, deux). When the next word starts with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u, or a silent h), that consonant wakes up and is pronounced as the first sound of the next word: vous avez sounds like 'vou-ZA-vé'. Written s and x link as a z sound, d links as a t sound, and n links as n while the vowel before it keeps its nasal ring. Listen for the linking sound: it is often the only thing that tells you a word is plural (les amis 'lé-ZA-mi').

examples.note: The silent s of vous becomes a z sound that starts avez: 'vou-ZA-vé'. Without it, a French ear hears two separate, clumsy words.
'lé-ZAN-fan': the linking z is the only audible plural marker, because the s of enfants is silent.
The silent t of petit is pronounced before ami: 'peu-ti-TA-mi'. Compare un petit chien, where the t stays silent.
A final d links as a t sound: 'gran-TÔ-tel'. The h of hôtel is silent, so liaison happens exactly as before a vowel.

contrast.note: Never link after et (and): say 'é An', not 'é-TAN'. Linking here would make it sound like est (is).
Some h-words (haricot, hors-d'oeuvre, huit) block liaison: 'lé a-ri-ko', with a tiny break instead of 'lé-ZA-ri-ko'.
No liaison before a consonant: the t of est stays silent because parti starts with p. Liaison only happens before a vowel sound.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers pronounce each word separately ('vous / avez', 'les / amis') so the plural and the flow disappear; carry the final consonant over as the first sound of the next vowel word: vou-za-vé, lé-za-mi.

probes.en: the s links as a z: 'vou-za-vé'
options: the s is pronounced as s: 'vou-sa-vé'
the v of avez is dropped: 'vou-zé'

probes.en: the d links as a t: 'gran-tô-tel'
probes.ex: Ils travaillent dans un grand hôtel.
probes.exEn: They work in a big hotel.
options: the d links as a d: 'gran-dô-tel'
the t links as a d: 'é-dan'
et and Anne merge into one syllable

items.note: The silent s of vous is pronounced as a z that starts avez: 'vou-ZA-vé'; keep your tongue in the z position and slide straight into the a.
items.ex: Est-ce que vous avez un stylo ?

items.note: Same z link as vous avez: 'nou-ZA-von'; the final -ons is a nasal 'on' with no n at the end.
items.ex: Ce soir, nous avons des invités.

items.note: 'lé-ZA-mi': the linking z is the only sound that tells you it is plural, since the s of amis is silent; without the z, nothing tells the listener there is more than one friend.
items.ex: Je dîne avec les amis de Marie.
items.exEn: I'm having dinner with Marie's friends.

items.note: The n of un links: 'un-NA-mi'. Keep the nasal 'un' sound, then add a clear n as the first sound of ami.
items.ex: Marc est un ami de mon frère.
items.exEn: Marc is a friend of my brother's.

items.note: The silent t of petit is pronounced before the vowel of ami: 'peu-ti-TA-mi'. Literally 'little friend', it is the everyday word for boyfriend.
items.ex: Je te présente mon petit ami.

items.en: it is a / he is a
items.note: The t of est links to un: 'sè-TUN'. This is one of the most frequent liaisons in French, so it is a great one to copy from day one.
A final x links as a z sound: 'deu-ZEUR'. The h of heures is silent, so liaison behaves exactly as before a vowel.
'trwa-ZAN': the s of trois links as z, and ans keeps its nasal 'an' sound with no n pronounced at the end.
A final d links as a t, not a d: 'gran-TÔ-tel'. The h of hôtel is a silent 'h muet', which allows the link.
items.ex: Nous dormons dans un grand hôtel.
items.exEn: We are sleeping in a big hotel.

items.note: The n of en links: 'an-NÉ-té'. Keep the nasal 'an' of en, then pronounce a real n to start été.
items.ex: Je vais à la plage en été.
items.exEn: I go to the beach in summer.

items.note: The silent s of très becomes z: 'trè-ZIM-por-tan'. Liaison after très, plus, and bien before a vowel is compulsory in careful speech.
A forbidden liaison: the t of et is never pronounced, so say 'é el' with a tiny break. Linking would make it sound like est (is).

teaching.rule: Connectors are the small words that glue two ideas together so you can say more than one sentence at a time. Learn each one by its job: et joins (and), ou offers a choice (or), mais contrasts (but), parce que gives a reason (because), donc and alors give a result (so). To tell a story in order use d'abord (first), puis or ensuite (then / next) and enfin (finally). Most of them go exactly where the English word goes, so the hard part is just remembering the sound: et is said 'é' with a silent t, and parce que shrinks to parce qu' before a vowel.

examples.fr: Je prends du pain et du fromage.
examples.note: et links two items; its t is never pronounced, even before a vowel.
mais introduces the contrast, like English 'but'.

examples.fr: Je reste parce que je suis fatigué.
examples.note: parce que gives the reason and is two words, never 'pourquoi', which asks the question.

examples.fr: Il pleut, donc je prends un parapluie.
examples.en: It's raining, so I'm taking an umbrella.
examples.note: donc gives the logical result of the first half.

examples.fr: D'abord on mange, puis on sort.
examples.en: First we eat, then we go out.
examples.note: d'abord opens the sequence, puis moves to the next step.

contrast.note: NOT 'parce que il pleut': que loses its e before a vowel and becomes qu'.

contrast.fr: Pourquoi tu restes ? Parce que je suis fatigué.
contrast.en: Why are you staying? Because I'm tired.
contrast.note: pourquoi asks the question; parce que answers it. They are not interchangeable.
NOT 'où' with an accent: ou means 'or', où means 'where'; only the accent separates them.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers say 'parce que il' or write 'ou' for 'where'; shrink parce que to parce qu' before a vowel, and remember ou = or, où = where.

probes.fr: ___ on mange, puis on sort, et enfin on rentre.
probes.ex: D'abord on mange, puis on sort, et enfin on rentre.
probes.exEn: First we eat, then we go out, and finally we go home.

items.note: Joins two words or ideas; pronounced 'é' with a silent t, and it never links to a following vowel.
items.ex: Je prends du pain et du fromage.

items.note: Introduces a contrast; in speech it often starts a reply ('Mais non !').
items.ex: C'est cher, mais c'est très bon.
items.exEn: It's expensive, but it's very good.

items.note: Offers a choice; no accent, unlike où (where).
items.ex: Tu veux du thé ou du café ?
items.exEn: Do you want tea or coffee?

items.note: Two words that give a reason; before a vowel que shrinks to qu' (parce qu'il).
items.ex: Je reste à la maison parce que je suis fatigué.
items.exEn: I'm staying home because I'm tired.

items.note: States a logical result; slightly more formal than alors, and the c is pronounced.
items.ex: Il pleut, donc je prends un parapluie.
items.exEn: It's raining, so I'm taking an umbrella.

items.note: The everyday spoken 'so': it can give a result or just open a sentence ('Alors, on y va ?').
items.ex: Je suis fatigué, alors je rentre.
items.exEn: I'm tired, so I'm going home.

items.note: Adds something to what was just said; in 'Moi aussi' it means 'me too'.
Opens a sequence of steps; the d' is a shrunken de and is always attached.
items.exEn: First of all we have a coffee.

items.note: Moves the story to the next step; the s is silent.
items.ex: Je mange, puis je vais au travail.
items.exEn: I eat, then I go to work.

items.note: Same job as puis but a bit fuller; handy when you are listing several steps.
items.ex: On visite le musée, ensuite on déjeune.
items.exEn: We visit the museum, after that we have lunch.

items.note: Closes a sequence or shows relief that something has happened at last.
items.ex: Après deux heures de route, on arrive enfin !
items.exEn: After two hours on the road, we finally arrive!

items.note: Introduces an illustration of what you just said; the x of exemple is pronounced 'gz'.
items.ex: J'aime les fruits, par exemple les pommes.
items.exEn: I like fruit, for example apples.

teaching.rule: The imparfait is the past tense for how things WERE: descriptions (it was sunny, I was tired), habits (we used to go every summer), and actions that were going on in the background (I was reading). To form it, take the 'nous' form of the present, drop -ons, and add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient: nous parlons gives je parlais, tu parlais, il parlait, nous parlions, vous parliez, ils parlaient. The only irregular stem is être: ét- (j'étais). Listen for the '-ai' sound at the end of the verb; the je, tu, il and ils forms all sound the same.

examples.fr: Quand j'étais petit, j'habitais à Lyon.
examples.en: When I was little, I lived in Lyon.
examples.note: A description of a past situation, not a single event: both verbs are imparfait.

examples.fr: Il faisait beau et les enfants jouaient dehors.
examples.en: The weather was nice and the children were playing outside.
examples.note: Scene-setting: weather and an ongoing activity. Faire gives fais- from nous faisons.

examples.fr: Chaque été, on allait à la mer.
examples.en: Every summer we used to go to the sea.
examples.note: A repeated habit ('used to') takes the imparfait; the stem all- comes from nous allons.

examples.fr: Nous finissions nos devoirs à 18 h.
examples.en: We used to finish our homework at 6 pm.
examples.note: -ir verbs like finir have a long stem finiss- from nous finissons.

contrast.note: One completed event that happened once is passé composé, not imparfait.
Present tense; the imparfait version is j'étais fatigué, 'I was tired'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers build the imparfait from the je form of the present (giving forms like 'je finais'); always start from the nous form minus -ons (nous finissons gives je finissais).

probes.exEn: She was singing in the shower.

probes.ex: Quand j'étais petit, j'adorais le chocolat.
probes.exEn: When I was little, I loved chocolate.

items.note: Être is the one verb with an irregular imparfait stem, ét-; it describes a past state, not an event.
The imparfait of c'est; the go-to way to describe or judge something in the past ('it was great').
Il y a in the past: avoir gives av- from nous avons, plus -ait; it also means 'there were', as it never changes for plural.
items.ex: Il y avait beaucoup de monde.
items.exEn: There were a lot of people.

items.note: Weather in the past is almost always imparfait because it describes the background; the stem fais- comes from nous faisons.
items.ex: Hier, il faisait beau et chaud.
items.exEn: Yesterday the weather was nice and hot.

items.note: Pleuvoir only exists in the il form; pleuv- plus -ait paints the rainy background of a story.
items.ex: Il pleuvait quand nous sommes sortis.
items.exEn: It was raining when we went out.

items.note: Avoir: av- plus -ions; the nous and vous endings are -ions and -iez, with a clear 'y' sound.
items.ex: À l'époque, nous avions un chien.
items.exEn: Back then, we had a dog.

items.note: Regular -er verb: parl- from nous parlons plus -ais; it describes what was in progress when something else happened.
items.ex: Je parlais avec Marc quand tu as appelé.
items.exEn: I was talking with Marc when you called.

items.note: The ils ending -aient looks long but sounds exactly like -ais and -ait; only the spelling shows the plural.
items.ex: Les enfants jouaient dans le jardin.
items.exEn: The children were playing in the garden.

items.note: Vouloir: voul- from nous voulons plus -iez; wanting is a state, so past 'wanted' is usually imparfait.
Aller: all- from nous allons plus -ait; with a time phrase like le dimanche or chaque été the imparfait means 'used to'.
items.ex: Le dimanche, on allait chez ma grand-mère.
items.exEn: On Sundays we used to go to my grandmother's.

items.note: Manger keeps its extra -e only before a and o (je mangeais, nous mangeons); before -ions it drops it: mangions.
items.ex: Nous mangions quand il est arrivé.
items.exEn: We were eating when he arrived.

items.note: Regular -ir verbs take the long stem from nous finissons: finiss- plus -ais.
items.ex: Je finissais mes devoirs quand tu es rentré.
items.exEn: I was finishing my homework when you came home.

teaching.rule: When you tell a story about the past, use the passé composé for the EVENTS, the things that happened and moved the story forward (the phone rang, I fell, she left), and the imparfait for the BACKGROUND, how things were and what was going on (it was raining, I was sleeping, we used to go). Time words help you choose: 'tout à coup', 'soudain', 'un jour', 'ce jour-là' point to a passé composé event; 'd'habitude', 'tous les jours', 'à l'époque', 'pendant que' point to imparfait background ('hier' alone can open either). A single sentence often has both: 'Je dormais (background) quand le téléphone a sonné (event).'

examples.fr: Je dormais quand le téléphone a sonné.
examples.en: I was sleeping when the phone rang.
examples.note: Sleeping is the ongoing background (imparfait); the ring is the sudden event (passé composé).

examples.fr: D'habitude, je prenais le bus, mais ce jour-là j'ai pris un taxi.
examples.en: Usually I took the bus, but that day I took a taxi.
examples.note: Habit = imparfait; the one-off exception on a specific day = passé composé.

examples.fr: Il faisait froid, alors j'ai fermé la fenêtre.
examples.en: It was cold, so I closed the window.
examples.note: The cold is a description (imparfait); closing the window is what I did about it (passé composé).

examples.fr: Elle avait 20 ans quand elle a rencontré Marc.
examples.en: She was 20 when she met Marc.
examples.note: Age is a state (imparfait); the meeting is a datable event (passé composé).

contrast.fr: Hier, il pleuvait toute la journée. / Hier, il a plu toute la journée.
contrast.en: Yesterday it was raining all day. / Yesterday it rained all day.
contrast.note: Both are correct: the imparfait paints the scene, the passé composé reports the day's rain as a finished fact.
'Soudain' announces an event, so French wants the passé composé: Soudain, il a commencé à pleuvoir.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers use the passé composé for everything in the past because English 'I did' covers both; ask 'did it happen once, or was it the situation?' and give the situation the imparfait.

probes.fr: Je lisais quand elle est arrivée.
probes.en: I was reading when she arrived.
probes.ex: Je lisais quand elle est arrivée.
probes.exEn: I was reading when she arrived.
options: I had read before she arrived.

probes.ex: Soudain, il a commencé à pleuvoir.
Il faisait beau, alors nous sommes sortis.
probes.exEn: The weather was nice, so we went out.

items.note: Signals a sudden event, so the verb that follows is in the passé composé.
items.ex: Tout à coup, la lumière s'est éteinte.

items.note: Introduces the moment something happened in a story; the verb after it is passé composé.
items.ex: Un jour, elle a décidé de partir.
items.exEn: One day, she decided to leave.

items.note: Points to one specific day, so it goes with a passé composé event; the -là is attached with a hyphen.
items.ex: Ce jour-là, j'ai rencontré ma femme.
items.exEn: That day, I met my wife.

items.note: Announces a habit, so the past verb after it is imparfait ('used to').
Repeated action; in the past it calls for the imparfait, because it is a routine rather than one event.
items.ex: Tous les jours, il marchait jusqu'à l'école.
items.exEn: Every day, he walked to school.

items.note: Sets a whole past period as background, so the description that follows is imparfait.
items.ex: À l'époque, on n'avait pas de portable.
items.exEn: Back then, we didn't have mobile phones.

items.note: Introduces the ongoing background action in the imparfait; the interrupting event is passé composé.
items.ex: Pendant que je lisais, il a téléphoné.
items.exEn: While I was reading, he phoned.

items.note: Every fairy tale opens with the imparfait of être, because it sets the scene before anything happens.
items.ex: Il était une fois une princesse.
items.exEn: Once upon a time there was a princess.

items.note: Fear as a lasting state uses avoir in the imparfait (avais); French says 'to have fear'.
items.exEn: As a child, I was afraid of the dark.

items.note: The same expression in the passé composé means the fear started at one moment, a reaction to an event.
items.ex: Quand j'ai vu le chien, j'ai eu peur.
items.exEn: When I saw the dog, I got scared.

items.note: Passé composé of pleuvoir (plu): the rain is reported as a finished fact with a limit, here two hours.
items.ex: Hier, il a plu pendant deux heures.
items.exEn: Yesterday it rained for two hours.

items.note: Falling is a sudden event, so passé composé; tomber takes être, and the participle agrees (tombée for a woman).
items.ex: Je courais et je suis tombé.
items.exEn: I was running and I fell.

items.note: Background action in progress (imparfait): it was going on when something else happened and interrupted it.
items.ex: Je dormais quand tu as appelé.
items.exEn: I was sleeping when you called.

items.note: A sudden event that moves the story forward, so passé composé (a sonné), even though the action around it is imparfait.
items.ex: Je prenais ma douche quand le téléphone a sonné.
items.exEn: I was taking a shower when the phone rang.

teaching.rule: An object pronoun replaces the person or thing a verb acts on, so you don't repeat it: 'Marie ? Je la vois demain.' Choose the pronoun by asking whether the verb takes 'à' before its object. No 'à' (direct): me, te, le, la, l', nous, vous, les. With 'à' (indirect, as in parler à, téléphoner à): me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur. Unlike English, the pronoun goes BEFORE the verb (Je le vois, not Je vois le), and in the passé composé it goes before avoir: Je l'ai vu.

examples.fr: Tu connais Paul ? Oui, je le connais.
examples.en: Do you know Paul? Yes, I know him.
examples.note: Connaître has no 'à', so Paul is a direct object: le. It sits before the verb.

examples.fr: Tu parles à Marie ? Oui, je lui parle.
examples.en: Are you talking to Marie? Yes, I'm talking to her.
examples.note: Parler à has 'à', so Marie is indirect: lui, which means 'to him' or 'to her'.

examples.fr: Les clés ? Je les ai perdues.
examples.note: Les goes before the helper verb ai; perdues adds -es because les (the keys) is feminine plural and comes before.

examples.fr: Je vais leur téléphoner ce soir.
examples.en: I'm going to phone them tonight.
examples.note: Téléphoner à takes 'à', so leur (to them); with two verbs the pronoun goes before the second, unconjugated one.

contrast.note: English word order; in French the pronoun comes first: Je le vois.
Parler takes 'à' (parler à quelqu'un), so it needs the indirect pronoun: Je lui parle.
The pronoun leur never takes -s; leurs with -s is only the possessive (leurs enfants).

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers put the pronoun after the verb ('je vois le') and use le/la for 'to him/her'; put the pronoun before the verb and use lui/leur whenever the verb takes 'à'.

probes.exEn: I explain the rule to them.

probes.ex: Ta sœur ? Je la vois souvent.
probes.exEn: Your sister? I see her often.

items.note: Le replaces a masculine person or thing that the verb acts on directly (no 'à'); it goes before the verb.
La replaces a feminine direct object; connaître takes no 'à', so it is direct.
items.ex: Marie ? Oui, je la connais bien.
items.exEn: Marie? Yes, I know her well.

items.note: Le and la both shrink to l' before a vowel sound, so you cannot tell the gender from the pronoun alone.
items.exEn: This film, I love it a lot.

items.note: Les replaces any plural direct object, masculine or feminine; it stays before the verb.
items.ex: Ces pommes ? Je les achète au marché.
items.exEn: These apples? I buy them at the market.

items.note: Parler à takes 'à', so its object is indirect: lui, which covers both 'to him' and 'to her'.
items.ex: Mon frère ? Je lui parle tous les jours.
items.exEn: My brother? I talk to him every day.

items.note: Téléphoner à takes 'à', so 'to them' is leur, with no -s (leurs is the possessive).
items.ex: Mes parents ? Je leur téléphone le dimanche.
items.exEn: My parents? I phone them on Sundays.

items.note: Me is the object form of je; regarder is direct in French even though English says 'look AT'.
items.exEn: Why is he looking at me?

items.note: Te is the object form of tu; it becomes t' before a vowel (je t'aime).
items.exEn: OK, I believe you. (to a friend)

items.note: Nous is both subject 'we' and object 'us'; you know it is the object because another subject (Luc, il) comes before it.
items.ex: Luc nous invite à dîner samedi.
items.exEn: Luc is inviting us to dinner on Saturday.

items.en: I'm listening to you (formal, or to several people)
items.note: Vous is also both subject and object; écouter is direct in French although English adds 'to'.
items.exEn: Go ahead, I'm listening to you.

items.note: In the passé composé the pronoun goes before ai, and the past participle adds -e because the direct object (her) comes before the verb.
Dire à takes 'à', so lui; with aller + infinitive the pronoun sits before the infinitive, not before vais.
items.ex: Ne t'inquiète pas, je vais lui dire.
items.exEn: Don't worry, I'm going to tell him.

teaching.rule: 'Il faut que' means 'it is necessary that' and is the everyday way to say someone must do something: Il faut que je parte, 'I have to leave'. After 'il faut que' the verb switches to a special form called the subjunctive. To make it, take the ils form of the present, drop -ent, and add -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent: ils finissent gives que je finisse, que tu finisses, qu'il finisse. For regular -er verbs the je/tu/il forms sound just like the present, so you only hear the change with common irregulars: être (sois, soit), avoir (aie, ait), aller (aille), faire (fasse), pouvoir (puisse), savoir (sache), venir (vienne). For most verbs the nous and vous forms look like the imparfait (que nous allions, que vous partiez); verbs with a special stem keep it there too (soyons, ayons, fassions, puissions).

examples.note: Il faut que + subjunctive; partir gives part- from ils partent, plus -e.

examples.fr: Il faut que tu sois à l'heure.
examples.en: You have to be on time.
examples.note: Être is irregular: sois, sois, soit, soyons, soyez, soient.
Faire has the special stem fass-; que becomes qu' before a vowel.

examples.fr: Il faut que nous allions à la banque.
examples.en: We have to go to the bank.
examples.note: Aller: aille in the singular, but allions/alliez for nous/vous, same spelling as the imparfait.

contrast.en: One has to leave. / We need to leave.
contrast.note: Without 'que' there is no subjunctive: il faut + infinitive gives a general 'must' with no named person.

contrast.fr: Il faut que tu es là.
contrast.note: 'Es' is the ordinary present; after il faut que it must be the subjunctive: sois.
Devoir + infinitive says the same thing without any subjunctive; il faut que is simply more common in speech.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers keep the normal present after il faut que ('il faut que tu es'); the que triggers a change, so learn the irregular subjunctives (sois, ait, aille, fasse, puisse, sache) as a set.

probes.fr: Il faut que je ___ (faire) mes devoirs.
probes.ex: Il faut que je fasse mes devoirs.
probes.exEn: I have to do my homework.

probes.fr: Il faut que tu sois gentil.
probes.ex: Il faut que tu sois gentil avec ta sœur.
probes.exEn: You have to be nice to your sister.

probes.fr: Il faut que nous ___ (avoir) le temps.
probes.ex: Il faut que nous ayons le temps.
probes.exEn: We need to have the time.

items.en: it is necessary that / (someone) has to
items.note: The most common trigger of the subjunctive; the 'que' is what forces the next verb into its special form.
items.ex: Il faut que tu manges quelque chose.

items.note: The negative wraps around faut (ne faut pas) and still keeps que, so the subjunctive still follows.
items.ex: Il ne faut pas que tu oublies.

items.note: Partir: ils partent minus -ent gives part-, plus -e; the subjunctive je form ends in -e, not -s.
items.ex: Il faut que je parte maintenant.

items.note: Regular -ir verb: the stem finiss- from ils finissent plus -e; it sounds different from the present je finis.
items.ex: Il faut que je finisse ce travail.
items.exEn: I have to finish this work.

items.note: Être is fully irregular in the subjunctive: sois, sois, soit, soyons, soyez, soient.
items.ex: Il faut que tu sois là à 8 h.
items.exEn: You have to be there at 8.

items.note: Avoir is irregular: aie, aies, ait, ayons, ayez, aient; ait sounds like 'est', and its t is only heard in liaison before a vowel (qu'il ait un).
items.ex: Il faut qu'il ait un passeport.
items.exEn: He needs to have a passport.

items.note: Aller has the special stem aill- in the singular and ils forms; j'aille is written with the apostrophe because aille starts with a vowel.
items.ex: Il faut que j'aille chez le médecin.
items.exEn: I have to go to the doctor.

items.note: Faire uses the stem fass- in every subjunctive form; vous adds -iez.
items.ex: Il faut que vous fassiez attention.

items.note: Pouvoir has the special stem puiss-; after il faut que the present peux/peut is never used.
items.ex: Il faut que je puisse dormir.
items.exEn: I need to be able to sleep.

items.note: Savoir has the special stem sach-; tu adds -es.
items.ex: Il faut que tu saches la vérité.
items.exEn: You need to know the truth.

items.note: Venir: ils viennent minus -ent gives vienn-, plus -ent; the ils form is identical to the present.
Prendre: ils prennent gives prenn-, plus -es; the double n and the -es ending show it is subjunctive, not the present prends.
items.ex: Il faut que tu prennes le train de 8 h.
items.exEn: You have to take the 8 o'clock train.

teaching.rule: French splits English 'to know' into two verbs. Use savoir for facts and skills: it is followed by a little clause (que 'that', où 'where', si 'if', comment 'how') or by another verb (Je sais nager = I can swim). Use connaître for people, places and things you are familiar with: it is always followed directly by a noun (Je connais Paris, Je connais ta sœur). Quick test: if you can put 'that' or 'how to' after 'know' in English, it is savoir; if 'know' means 'be acquainted with', it is connaître. One nuance: savoir can also take a noun that stands for a piece of information you could recite (savoir la vérité, savoir son nom, savoir un poème par cœur).

examples.fr: Je sais que tu as raison.
examples.note: A fact introduced by que ('that'), so savoir: je sais.
savoir + verb = a learned skill; French does not add 'how to', the verb follows directly.
A place you are familiar with, followed directly by a noun, so connaître.
A person is always connaître, never savoir.

contrast.note: NOT 'Je sais ce restaurant': a place or person you are familiar with takes connaître; savoir is for facts and skills, not for places or people.
NOT 'Je connais où il habite': connaître can never be followed by où / que / si, only by a noun.
NOT 'Je connais nager' and NOT 'Je peux nager' for a skill you learned: savoir + verb means you know how.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers reach for connaître whenever they see 'know'; the fix is to check what follows: a clause or a verb means savoir, a person or place means connaître.

probes.ex: Vous savez où est la poste ?
probes.exEn: Do you know where the post office is?

items.note: savoir is for facts: it is followed by que 'that', où 'where', si 'if' or a verb, never by a person.
items.ex: Je sais que le magasin ferme à 19 h.
items.exEn: I know that the shop closes at 7 pm.

items.note: connaître is for people, places and things you have met or visited; it is followed directly by a noun.

items.en: to know (a fact or how to)
items.note: The dictionary form; irregular in the present (je sais, tu sais, il sait, nous savons, vous savez, ils savent). Here it takes la vérité directly because the truth is a piece of information, not a person or place.
items.exEn: Do you want to know the truth?

items.note: The dictionary form; the î keeps its hat only before t (il connaît), and the verb is always followed by a noun.
items.exEn: I'd like to get to know your friends.

items.note: savoir + verb means a learned skill; French drops the words 'how to' and puts the verb straight after sait.
items.ex: Ma fille sait nager depuis l'été dernier.
items.exEn: My daughter has been able to swim since last summer.

items.note: tu sais opens a question about a fact (où, quand, comment, si); the s at the end is silent.
items.ex: Tu sais où est la gare ?
items.exEn: Do you know where the station is?

items.note: Use tu connais when 'know' means you have been somewhere or met someone; a place or person follows directly.
The plural stem doubles the s (connaiss-) and the -ent ending is silent, so it sounds like 'ko-ness'.
items.ex: Ils connaissent mes parents depuis dix ans.
items.exEn: They've known my parents for ten years.

items.note: The everyday 'no idea' answer uses savoir because you are talking about a fact; in fast speech it shrinks to 'je sais pas' or 'chais pas'.
items.ex: Où est Paul ? Je ne sais pas.

items.note: A set phrase built on connaître (familiarity): the y is fixed, and en introduces the field you know well.
items.ex: Mon oncle s'y connaît en vin.
items.exEn: My uncle knows a lot about wine.

items.note: Something learned 'by heart' usually goes with savoir (a memorised text is information you can recite); connaître par cœur is also heard, so both are fine.
items.ex: Elle sait le poème par cœur.
items.exEn: She knows the poem by heart.

items.note: re + connaître = to 'know again'; it belongs to the familiarity family, so it takes a noun directly, like connaître.
items.ex: Je ne reconnais pas cette rue.

teaching.rule: Real French conversation is glued together with little words that carry almost no meaning but make you sound natural: du coup ('so'), en fait ('actually'), bref ('anyway'), quoi tagged at the end of a sentence ('you know'), hein for 'right?', and euh when you need a second to think. They belong in speech and text messages, not in a formal email. Listen for them at the start or the very end of a sentence, and copy one or two at a time; overusing them sounds as odd in French as saying 'like' in every sentence does in English.

examples.fr: Il pleuvait, du coup on est restés à la maison.
examples.en: It was raining, so we stayed home.
examples.note: du coup links a cause to its result in casual speech; among friends it is heard far more often than donc.

examples.en: It's a bit expensive, you know.
examples.note: quoi at the end of a sentence sums up or softens what you just said; it is never a question here.

examples.fr: En fait, je préfère le thé.
examples.note: en fait corrects or adds a detail, like English 'actually'; do not confuse it with en effet ('indeed') or au fait ('by the way').
hein asks for agreement, like an English tag question; it always comes with a rising voice.

contrast.note: NOT 'Brièvement' or 'En bref' in speech: bref alone is the natural way to cut a story short.

contrast.fr: Euh... je ne sais pas trop.
contrast.note: NOT the English 'um' or 'uh': French thinking noises are euh (an 'uh' with rounded lips) and ben.

contrast.fr: Du coup, tu viens ce soir ?
contrast.note: donc is correct but neutral; among friends du coup is the usual choice, and it is never spelled 'du coût'.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers translate 'actually' as actuellement (which means 'currently') and never pick up du coup; in conversation say en fait for 'actually' and du coup for 'so'.

probes.fr: Il pleuvait, ___ on est restés à la maison.
probes.ex: Il pleuvait, du coup on est restés à la maison.
probes.exEn: It was raining, so we stayed home.
Anyway, it was a long day.

items.note: The most common spoken connector for cause and result; it belongs in conversation and texts, not in formal writing.
items.ex: Le bus était en retard, du coup j'ai pris un taxi.
items.exEn: The bus was late, so I took a taxi.

items.note: Tacked on at the very end of a sentence after a comma, quoi wraps up or softens what you said; it is not the question word here.
items.exEn: It's a good film, you know.

items.note: bon ben (often written 'bon, ben') opens a sentence when you move on or give in; ben is a lazy 'bien' said with a nasal vowel.
items.exEn: Well then, I'm going to head home.

items.note: One word that cuts a story short and jumps to the point; say it at the start of the sentence with a small pause after it.
items.ex: Bref, on a raté le train.

items.note: The French hesitation noise: say 'uh' but with rounded lips; using English 'um' instantly marks you as a foreigner.
items.ex: Euh... je crois que c'est fermé.

items.note: Used to correct or add a detail; the final t is pronounced (say 'ahn-fett'); do not confuse it with en effet ('indeed') or au fait ('by the way').
items.ex: En fait, je ne suis pas libre samedi.
items.exEn: Actually, I'm not free on Saturday.

items.note: Literally 'you see'; friends drop it into a sentence to check you are following, the way English uses 'you know'.
Very informal, mostly under-40s: genre means 'like' or 'roughly' before a detail; its literal meaning is 'kind / type'.
items.ex: Il est arrivé genre à minuit.
items.exEn: He got there, like, at midnight.

items.note: Adds a shrug of 'even so'; the d of quand is silent and même carries the stress (say 'kan-mem').
Opens an opinion you want taken seriously; the -ment ending is the French '-ly' and is nasal.
A nasal sound (like the vowel of vin, through the nose) at the end of a sentence that asks for agreement; on its own with a rising tone it means 'what?' and is a bit rude.
The relaxed spoken version of oui, said 'way'; fine with friends, but answer oui to a boss or an official.

teaching.rule: An idiom is a fixed phrase whose meaning you cannot guess word by word: poser un lapin literally means 'to put down a rabbit' but really means 'to stand someone up'. Learn each one as a whole chunk with its little words (le, des, dans) exactly as given, and only swap the verb ending to match the person (j'ai le cafard, elle a le cafard). Many are built on avoir ('to have') or être ('to be'), and most are everyday casual speech, so listen for them among friends and use them there.

examples.note: Literally 'I have the cockroach': a set phrase with avoir, and le cafard never changes.
Literally 'it's raining ropes', the French version of cats and dogs.

examples.fr: Ça coûte les yeux de la tête.
examples.en: It costs an arm and a leg.
examples.note: Literally 'the eyes of the head'; the body part differs from English, so translate the meaning, not the words.

examples.fr: Le dimanche, je fais la grasse matinée.
examples.note: Literally 'to do the fat morning'; faire is the verb that changes (tu fais, il fait), the rest stays fixed.

contrast.note: NOT a real rabbit and NOT 'il m'a laissé debout': the English words for standing up never appear in the French idiom.

contrast.fr: C'est pas la mer à boire.
contrast.note: NOT 'ce n'est pas si dur' when you want to sound natural, and NOT 'pas de la mer': the à is part of the fixed phrase.

contrast.fr: Elle est tombée dans les pommes.
contrast.note: NOT 'elle a fainté': the English verb does not exist in French; the idiom, or s'évanouir, does the job.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers translate their own idioms word for word ('il pleut des chats et des chiens'), which means nothing to a French listener; learn the French chunk as-is and only change the verb ending.

probes.ex: Ça coûte les yeux de la tête.
probes.exEn: It costs an arm and a leg.

probes.ex: Depuis la rentrée, il a le cafard.
probes.exEn: He has been feeling down since the start of the school year.

items.note: Literally 'to have the cockroach'; built on avoir, so only the verb changes (j'ai, tu as, elle a) and le cafard stays fixed.
items.exEn: I've been feeling down since Monday.

items.fr: coûter les yeux de la tête
items.en: to cost an arm and a leg
items.note: Literally 'to cost the eyes of the head'; French picks eyes where English picks limbs, so learn the whole chunk.
items.ex: Cette voiture coûte les yeux de la tête.
items.exEn: This car costs an arm and a leg.
alts: couter les yeux de la tete

items.note: Literally 'to fall into the apples'; tomber takes être in the past (elle est tombée dans les pommes).
items.ex: Il fait si chaud que je vais tomber dans les pommes.
items.exEn: It's so hot I'm going to faint.

items.note: Literally 'to put down a rabbit'; the person stood up is the indirect object (il m'a posé un lapin = he stood ME up).
items.ex: Elle m'a encore posé un lapin.

items.note: Literally 'to have the peach'; the opposite of avoir le cafard, and just as fixed: only avoir changes.
items.exEn: This morning I'm full of energy!

items.fr: ce n'est pas la mer à boire
items.note: Literally 'it's not the sea to drink'; said to encourage someone, and in speech ne drops (c'est pas la mer à boire).
items.ex: Allez, ce n'est pas la mer à boire !
items.exEn: Come on, it's not that hard!
alts: c'est pas la mer à boire

items.en: to have one's head in the clouds
items.note: Literally 'to be in the moon'; French daydreamers are on the moon, English ones are in the clouds, so keep lune.
items.ex: Tu es encore dans la lune !
items.exEn: You've got your head in the clouds again!

items.fr: avoir un chat dans la gorge
items.en: to have a frog in one's throat
items.note: Literally 'to have a cat in the throat'; the animal changes between the languages, the meaning (a hoarse voice) does not.
items.ex: Excuse-moi, j'ai un chat dans la gorge.
items.exEn: Sorry, I've got a frog in my throat.

items.note: Literally 'it's raining ropes', the picture being thick lines of rain; des cordes is fixed, only pleut can change tense (il pleuvait des cordes).
items.ex: Prends un parapluie, il pleut des cordes.

items.note: Literally 'to do the fat morning'; faire is the only part that changes (je fais, on a fait la grasse matinée).
items.ex: Le dimanche, je fais la grasse matinée.

items.fr: avoir du pain sur la planche
