items.en: to have a lot on one's plate
items.note: Literally 'to have bread on the board'; French counts work in loaves, English in plates, so do not mix the images.
items.ex: Cette semaine, j'ai du pain sur la planche.
items.exEn: This week I have a lot on my plate.

items.en: let's get back to the point
items.note: Literally 'let's come back to our sheep', from a medieval play; said as a whole with nous-form revenons, usually after a digression.
items.exEn: Right, let's get back to the point.

teaching.rule: French marks respect not only with vous but with whole phrases and word choices. With a stranger, an official, a customer or your boss, use the polished forms: Pourriez-vous... ? instead of Tu peux... ?, Je vous remercie instead of merci, Veuillez + verb for written instructions, and Cordialement to close an email. With friends the same ideas come out shorter and with slang nouns (le boulot for le travail, un truc for une chose, un pote for un ami). Start every new relationship in the formal register and let the French speaker invite you to relax.

examples.note: The polite 'could you' form: pourriez-vous with the verb-subject flipped signals a formal request.
Veuillez is the formal written 'please do' you see on signs, in emails and on phone menus.

examples.fr: Je vous remercie de votre réponse.
examples.note: A full sentence is more formal than a bare merci; de introduces what you are thanking for.
Informal register: le boulot replaces le travail among friends and family; never write it to a client.

contrast.note: NOT 'Bisous' or 'À plus' at the end of a work email: those are for friends only.
NOT 'Cher Monsieur / Chère Madame' to a stranger: French usually saves 'cher' for people you already know; the bare titles are the safe opener.
NOT 'Je veux un café' to a waiter: je veux sounds like a demand; the would-like form is the polite default.

teaching.commonMistake: English speakers assume vous alone makes them polite and then say 'Je veux', 'merci' and 'boulot' to a stranger; match the whole sentence to the register with Je voudrais, Je vous remercie and le travail.

probes.exEn: Have a good day. Kind regards, Marc Dupont.

items.note: The standard opener of a formal letter or email to someone you do not know; French lists Madame first and adds no 'cher'.
items.ex: Madame, Monsieur, je vous écris au sujet de ma réservation.
items.exEn: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing about my booking.

items.note: The all-purpose sign-off for professional emails; Bien cordialement is a touch warmer, and neither is used with close friends.
items.exEn: Thanks in advance. Kind regards, Julie Martin.

items.note: A frozen command form of vouloir ('to want') meaning 'be so kind as to'; it is followed by a verb in the dictionary form and appears on signs, in emails and on phone lines.
items.ex: Veuillez laisser un message après le bip.
items.exEn: Please leave a message after the beep.

items.note: A full sentence built on remercier; more formal than merci and followed by de or pour to say what you are thanking for.
items.ex: Je vous remercie de votre aide.

items.note: The conditional ('would') form of pouvoir ('can') with vous flipped behind the verb; flipping the order is itself a marker of formality.
items.exEn: Could you send me the document?

items.note: The conditional ('would') form of avoir ('to have') with vous flipped behind; the polite way to ask whether something is available in a shop, hotel or restaurant.
items.exEn: Would you have a table for two?

items.note: The formal way to interrupt someone; de + verb names what you are apologising for, and déranger means 'to disturb'.
items.ex: Excusez-moi de vous déranger, madame, je cherche la sortie.
items.exEn: Sorry to bother you, madam, I'm looking for the exit.

items.note: The everyday slang for le travail, fine with friends and family; in an interview or an email to a client say le travail or le poste.
items.ex: Je vais au boulot à vélo.
items.exEn: I go to work by bike.

items.note: The casual stand-in for une chose or a word you cannot find; avoid it in formal writing, where une chose or the precise noun is expected.
items.ex: J'ai un truc à te dire.
items.exEn: I've got something to tell you.

items.note: Casual for un homme; also 'boyfriend' as mon mec. Use un homme or un monsieur when speaking to strangers or in writing.
The relaxed word for un ami, same form for men and women (une pote); say un ami or un collègue in formal settings.
Short for à plus tard, said 'a-pluss' with the s sounded; a sign-off for friends and texts, never for a professional email.
items.exEn: Right, I'm off, see you later!
